The other, a thoroughly gloomy man resting his hands and chin on a stick, felt entitled on the grounds of general merit, rather than any narrowly defined service. Both were irreproachable citizens of Brassing who wished Jonah Featherstone did not live there. A family’s wit is generally appreciated most by outsiders.

“Trumbull alone is pretty certain of five hundred—you can count on _that_. I wouldn’t be surprised if my brother promised it,” Solomon had reflected aloud to his sisters on the evening before the funeral.
“Dear me, dear me!” said poor sister Martha. Her habitual notion of hundreds had scarcely extended beyond the amount of rent she owed.

By morning, however, the appearance of an unknown mourner had upset every familiar line of speculation. He seemed to have splashed down among them from the moon. This was the man Mrs. Cadwallader called frog-faced: perhaps thirty-two or thirty-three, with protruding eyes, a thin-lipped mouth curved downward, and hair brushed smoothly back from a forehead which receded abruptly above the brows. His face certainly had a frog’s fixed expression. Here, plainly, was another beneficiary; why else invite him to mourn? New possibilities brought fresh uncertainty and almost silenced conversation in the mourning coaches. We all feel humbled by the sudden discovery of a fact that has existed quite comfortably, perhaps privately staring at us, while we have been constructing a world that leaves it out altogether. Nobody had previously seen this dubious stranger except Mary Garth. All she knew was that twice, when Mr. Featherstone was still coming downstairs, he had visited Stone Court and remained alone with him for several hours. She had managed to tell her father. Perhaps Caleb’s eyes, apart from the lawyer’s, were the only ones studying the stranger with curiosity rather than disgust or suspicion. Expecting little and coveting still less, Caleb Garth wanted to see whether his guesses would prove right. As the unknown mourner, whose name they gathered was Rigg, entered the paneled parlor and sat near the door to hear the will, Caleb rubbed his chin with a half-smile and cast intelligent glances at him much as he might appraise a tree. His composure contrasted strikingly with the alarm or contempt on other faces. Mr. Solomon and Mr. Jonah had just gone upstairs with the lawyer to find the will. Noticing two empty chairs between herself and Mr. Borthrop Trumbull, Mrs. Waule summoned the courage to move beside that great authority. He was fingering his watch seals and arranging his appearance, determined to betray neither wonder nor surprise—both so compromising to a man of ability.
“I expect you know all about what my poor brother’s arranged, Mr. Trumbull,” Mrs. Waule said in her softest muffled voice, turning her crape-shaded bonnet toward his ear.
“My dear lady, anything communicated to me was communicated in confidence,” the auctioneer answered, raising a hand as if to shield the secret.
“People who’ve counted on their good fortune may find themselves mistaken yet,” Mrs. Waule went on, somewhat relieved by saying so.
“Expectations frequently mislead us,” said Mr. Trumbull, maintaining their confidential tone.
“Ah!” Mrs. Waule looked across at the Vincys, then returned to the chair beside her sister Martha.

“Poor Peter was amazingly secretive,” she said, still in an undertone. “Not one of us knows what he may have had on his conscience. I only hope, Martha, his way of life wasn’t worse than we’ve supposed.”

Poor Mrs. Cranch was stout and asthmatic. She had an extra reason for keeping her observations harmless and general: even her whispers were loud and liable to erupt like a malfunctioning barrel organ.

“I’ve _never_ been grasping, Jane,” she replied. “But I have six children living and three buried, and my husband had no fortune. The eldest, sitting over there, is only nineteen—you can judge for yourself. Always short of stock, and such difficult land. But if I’ve begged and prayed to anyone, it’s been to God in heaven. Still, with one brother unmarried and the other childless after marrying twice, anyone might have thought!”

Meanwhile Mr. Vincy had looked at Mr. Rigg’s impassive face, taken out his snuffbox, and tapped it. Then he put it away unopened. Snuff might clear the judgment, but the occasion hardly suited such an indulgence. “Perhaps Featherstone had kinder feelings than any of us allowed,” he whispered to his wife. “This funeral suggests he thought about everybody. It’s a good sign when a man wants his friends to follow him, and isn’t ashamed of them because they’re humble. I’d be all the happier if he’s left plenty of little legacies. They can be immensely useful to people with small means.”
“It’s all been done as handsomely as possible—the crape, the silk, everything,” Mrs. Vincy said with satisfaction.

Fred, I regret to say, was having trouble suppressing laughter, which would have been still less appropriate than his father’s snuffbox. He had overheard Mr. Jonah mention a “love-child.” With that suggestion in his mind, the stranger’s face directly opposite seemed unbearably comic. Mary Garth noticed the twitching mouth and the refuge he took in coughing, and resourcefully rescued him by asking to exchange seats. This put him in a shadowy corner. Fred felt warmly disposed toward everyone, Rigg included. He was feeling especially charitable toward all these people, less fortunate than he knew himself to be, and would not for anything have misbehaved. Yet laughing was remarkably easy.

Everyone’s attention shifted when the lawyer returned with the two brothers. The lawyer, Mr. Standish, had arrived at Stone Court that morning believing he knew exactly who would be pleased and who disappointed before the day ended. He expected to read the last of three wills he had prepared for Mr. Featherstone. Mr. Standish never adjusted his manner to his company. His deep-voiced, casual politeness was the same for everyone, as though he recognized no distinctions. His chief topics were the hay crop, which would be “very fine, by God!”; the latest reports on the King’s health; and the Duke of Clarence, a sailor through and through and precisely the man to govern an island such as Britain.

Sitting before his fire, old Featherstone had often thought how surprised Standish would be one day. Certainly, if he had finally had his way and burned the will another lawyer had drawn up, he would have forfeited that minor satisfaction. But he had enjoyed turning it over in his mind. Mr. Standish was indeed surprised, though by no means sorry. On the contrary, discovering a second will gave his own curiosity a pleasant little stimulus, added to the prospect of watching the Featherstones’ astonishment.

Solomon’s and Jonah’s feelings, meanwhile, hung in complete uncertainty. They imagined the earlier will must retain some force, and that poor Peter’s earlier and later wishes might become so entangled that there would be endless “lawing” before anybody received his due. At least that inconvenience would be shared by all. They consequently came back with Mr. Standish wearing expressions of entirely neutral gravity. Solomon nevertheless brought out his white handkerchief again. Whatever happened, there would be touching passages; at funerals, even dry weeping was customarily presented in fine linen.

Perhaps Mary Garth’s heart beat with the greatest excitement just then. She knew that it was effectively her doing that this second will had survived to be produced, and that it might profoundly change the lives of people in the room. Not another soul knew what had happened on that last night.

“The will now in my hand,” said Mr. Standish, seated at the table in the center of the room and taking his time over everything, including the coughs with which he prepared to clear his voice, “was prepared by me and signed by our late friend on August 9, 1825. I have, however, discovered a later document, previously unknown to me, dated July 20, 1826—less than a year afterward. In addition, I find”—his spectacled eyes moved carefully over the paper—“a codicil to this later will, dated March 1, 1828.”
“Dear me, dear me!” said sister Martha. She had not intended to be heard, but the accumulation of dates forced an utterance out of her.
“I shall read the earlier will first,” Mr. Standish continued, “as the deceased evidently intended, since he did not destroy it.”

The opening formalities seemed rather lengthy. Several people besides Solomon shook their heads sorrowfully, looking down. Everyone avoided everyone else’s eyes. Most gazes rested on marks in the tablecloth or on Mr. Standish’s bald head. Mary Garth was the exception. Since all the others were trying to look nowhere, she could safely watch them. At the first “give and bequeath,” she saw their complexions change almost imperceptibly, as though a faint tremor had passed through them. Only Mr. Rigg remained exactly as before. Indeed, with more urgent questions to consider, and the difficulty of listening to gifts that might or might not have been withdrawn, the company had forgotten him. Fred reddened. Mr. Vincy could no longer resist holding his snuffbox, although he kept it shut.

The smaller legacies came first. Even remembering that there was another will, in which poor Peter might have reconsidered, could not prevent mounting disgust and indignation. We like people to treat us well in every tense: past, present, and future. Yet five years ago Peter had been capable of leaving his own brothers and sisters only two hundred each, and his nephews and nieces a mere hundred. The Garths were not mentioned. Mrs. Vincy and Rosamond were to receive a hundred apiece. Mr. Trumbull got the gold-headed cane and fifty pounds. The other second cousins and the cousins present each received the same handsome sum—a sort of legacy, as the gloomy cousin observed, that got a man nowhere. More of this insulting trickle was directed toward absent people, doubtful connections who, one feared, were socially low. A quick reckoning suggested about three thousand had been distributed. Where was the rest meant to go? And the land? What had been revoked, and what remained? Had the changes improved matters or made them worse? Every feeling must be provisional and might prove inappropriate. The men could endure this muddled suspense in silence, some dropping their lower lips, others pursing them, as their facial habits dictated. Jane and Martha, overwhelmed by the questions, began to weep. Poor Mrs. Cranch was half comforted by the prospect of receiving any hundreds without working for them, and half aware how small her share was. Mrs. Waule could think of nothing but being his own sister and getting little, while someone else would get a great deal. Everyone now expected that great deal to go to Fred Vincy. Even the Vincys were astonished, however, to hear ten thousand pounds in named investments left to him. Would the land follow? Fred bit his lips to keep from smiling. Mrs. Vincy felt herself the happiest woman alive; in this dazzling prospect, the possibility of revocation dwindled out of sight.

Personal property still remained, besides the land. All of it went to one person, and that person was—O possibilities! O hopes built on the favor of secretive old gentlemen! O endless exclamations, still powerless to measure human folly!—the beneficiary of everything remaining was Joshua Rigg. He was also appointed sole executor and required henceforth to take the surname Featherstone.
A rustle passed around the room like a shiver. Every eye returned to Mr. Rigg, who showed no sign of astonishment.

“An extraordinary disposition of property!” cried Mr. Trumbull, for once preferring to be thought previously uninformed. “But another will exists—a further document. The deceased’s final intentions have yet to be disclosed.”

Mary Garth knew that what they were about to hear did not express his final intentions. The second will canceled everything except the gifts to the socially humble people already mentioned—changes to some of these had occasioned the codicil—and the gift to Joshua Rigg of all the land in Lowick parish, together with the livestock and household furnishings. Everything else was to fund the building and endowment of homes for elderly men, to be called Featherstone’s Alms-Houses. They were to stand on land near Middlemarch which the testator had already bought for that purpose. His wish, the document stated, was to please God Almighty. Nobody there received a farthing, though Mr. Trumbull retained the gold-headed cane. For a time the company seemed unable to speak. Mary did not dare look at Fred.

Mr. Vincy spoke first, after energetic use of his snuffbox. His indignation was loud. “The most inexplicable will I’ve ever heard! I’d say he wasn’t in his right mind when he made it. I’d say this last will was invalid.” That word seemed to Mr. Vincy to put the matter in its proper light. “Wouldn’t you, Standish?”

“I believe our late friend always understood what he was doing,” Mr. Standish replied. “Everything is entirely in order. A letter from Clemmens of Brassing is tied to the will. He prepared it—a thoroughly reputable solicitor.”

“I observed no mental derangement, no disturbance of the intellect, in the late Mr. Featherstone,” Borthrop Trumbull said. “But I consider this will eccentric. I was always happy to assist the old gentleman. He indicated distinctly enough that he felt an obligation which his will would acknowledge. As an acknowledgment of my services, the gold-headed cane is absurd. Fortunately, financial motives are beneath me.”
“I can’t see anything particularly surprising,” said Caleb Garth. “A will such as you’d expect from an open, honest man would have been far more surprising. Personally, I wish wills didn’t exist.”
“By God, that’s an odd opinion for a Christian!” said the lawyer. “I’d like to hear how you defend that, Garth!”
“Well,” Caleb began, leaning forward, carefully arranging his fingertips and gazing thoughtfully at the floor. Words always seemed to him the most difficult part of business.

But Mr. Jonah Featherstone now made himself heard. “My brother Peter was always a first-rate hypocrite. This will beats everything, though. If I’d known, a wagon with six horses couldn’t have dragged me away from Brassing. Tomorrow I’m wearing a white hat and a drab coat.”

“Dear me, dear me,” Mrs. Cranch sobbed. “And all the money we’ve spent on coming here, and that poor boy kept idle so long! It’s the first I’ve heard of brother Peter being so eager to please God Almighty. If I were to be struck helpless for saying it, I’d still call it hard treatment. I can’t think otherwise.”

“It won’t help him where he’s gone, I believe,” said Solomon. The bitterness was strikingly sincere, though his tone could not stop sounding sly. “Peter led a bad life. Almshouses won’t conceal it, especially when he’s had the nerve to reveal it at the end.”

“When all along he had a proper lawful family of his own—brothers, sisters, nephews, nieces—and sat with us at church whenever he chose to attend,” Mrs. Waule added. “He could have left his property so respectably, to people who’ve never gone in for extravagance or wild living of any sort, and aren’t so poor they couldn’t save every penny and increase it. And the trouble I’ve taken, coming here over and over to behave like a sister! All the while he had things on his conscience to make your flesh crawl. If the Almighty has permitted it, He means to punish him. Brother Solomon, I’m ready to go, if you’ll drive me.”
“I’ve no wish ever to enter the place again,” Solomon replied. “I’ve land of my own, and property of my own to leave.”

“A sorry business, the way fortune deals with people,” said Jonah. “Having a little spirit never pays. Better to be a dog in the manger. Still, those of us above ground could take a lesson. One fool’s will is quite enough for any family.”

“There are several ways to be a fool,” Solomon said. “I won’t leave my money to be thrown down a drain, nor to foundlings from Africa. I prefer Featherstones born and bred, not people turned into Featherstones by having a name pasted on.”

Solomon delivered this loud aside to Mrs. Waule as he rose to leave with her. Jonah knew he could be far more cutting. But he reflected that insulting Stone Court’s new owner served no purpose until it was certain he had no intention of welcoming witty men whose name he was about to share.

Mr. Joshua Rigg, in fact, seemed little concerned by insinuations. His manner did change markedly, however: he walked composedly up to Mr. Standish and began asking practical questions with complete assurance. His voice was high and chirping, his accent atrocious. Fred, no longer tempted to laugh at him, thought him the most vulgar monster he had ever encountered. Fred felt rather sick. The Middlemarch fabric merchant waited for a chance to speak to Mr. Rigg. Who could tell how many pairs of legs the new owner might need stockings for? Profit was more dependable than an inheritance. Besides, as only a second cousin, the merchant was detached enough to feel curious.

After his first outburst, Mr. Vincy had maintained a proud silence. Unpleasant thoughts absorbed him so completely that he did not think of leaving until he saw his wife beside Fred, holding her darling’s hand and silently weeping. He got up immediately. Turning his back on the others, he murmured, “Steady, Lucy. Don’t make yourself foolish in front of these people, my dear.” Then he added in his ordinary loud voice, “Order the phaeton, Fred. I haven’t time to waste.”

Mary Garth had already been preparing to leave with her father. She met Fred in the hall and for the first time dared look at him. His face had the pinched pallor that sometimes comes over young faces, and the hand she shook was very cold. Mary was troubled too. She knew that, without intending it, she might have made a fatal difference to Fred’s prospects.
“Goodbye,” she said, sadly and tenderly. “Have courage, Fred. I really believe you’re better off without that money. What good did it do Mr. Featherstone?”

“That’s easy enough to say,” Fred answered irritably. “What am I supposed to do? Now I’ll have to enter the Church.” He knew this would annoy Mary; well, then she must suggest an alternative. “I’d expected to repay your father immediately and put everything right. And he hasn’t left you even a hundred pounds. What will you do now, Mary?”
“Find another position, of course, as soon as possible. Father has enough to do supporting the others, without keeping me. Goodbye.”

Very soon Stone Court was empty of genuine, home-brewed Featherstones and its other familiar visitors. Another stranger had come to settle near Middlemarch. In Mr. Rigg Featherstone’s case, however, people were more occupied with resenting the immediate, visible results than with speculating about his future influence. Nobody had enough prophetic insight to foresee what a trial of Joshua Rigg might bring to light.

At this point I am naturally drawn to consider how a low subject may be elevated. Historical parallels work remarkably well. Their chief disadvantage is that the conscientious narrator may lack space, or—which often amounts to the same thing—may be unable to recall any precisely, while remaining philosophically certain that, if known, they would illuminate the matter. A shorter, easier road to dignity might be this observation: no true story has ever existed that could not be told as a parable, with a monkey substituted for a margrave, or the reverse. Accordingly, everything I have narrated or shall narrate about humble people can be ennobled simply by treating it as a parable. Should bad habits and ugly consequences appear, the reader may take comfort in regarding their lack of refinement as merely figurative, and feel that he is effectively keeping quite fashionable company. Thus, even while I tell the truth about boors, my reader’s imagination need not be wholly deprived of lords. And those petty sums on which a bankrupt of distinction would disdain to retire can be raised to the scale of great commercial transactions by the inexpensive addition of a proportionate number of zeros.

As for a provincial history whose participants all possess lofty moral standing, that must belong to a time considerably later than the first Reform Bill. Peter Featherstone, you will observe, was already dead and buried several months before Lord Gray took office.

chapters.title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXVI
paragraphs:
’T is strange to see the humors of these men,
These great aspiring spirits, that should be wise:
. . . . . . . .
For being the nature of great spirits to love
To be where they may be most eminent;
They, rating of themselves so farre above
Us in conceit, with whom they do frequent,
Imagine how we wonder and esteeme
All that they do or say; which makes them strive
To make our admiration more extreme,
Which they suppose they cannot, ’less they give
Notice of their extreme and highest thoughts.
—DANIEL: _Tragedy of Philotas_.

Mr. Vincy came home from hearing the will with his views on many subjects considerably altered. He was a man open to impressions, but inclined to express himself indirectly. A disappointing market for his silk braids made him swear at the groom; annoyance with his brother-in-law Bulstrode produced cutting observations on Methodism. His newly stern view of Fred’s idleness now became apparent when he flung an embroidered cap out of the smoking room onto the hall floor.
“Well, sir,” he remarked as Fred headed for bed, “I hope you’ve decided to return next term and pass your examination. I’ve made up my mind, and I advise you not to waste time making up yours.”

Fred said nothing. He was too completely crushed. Twenty-four hours earlier, he had expected that by now he would no longer need to consider what to do: he would know that he need do nothing. He would hunt in a scarlet coat, own a first-rate hunter, ride to the meet on a fine hack, and earn general respect for it all. He would also repay Mr. Garth immediately, and Mary could have no further reason to refuse him. All this was supposed to happen without studying or any other inconvenience, through Providence’s kindness as embodied in an old gentleman’s whim. Now, at the end of those twenty-four hours, every confident expectation lay overturned. It seemed “rather hard lines” to be treated, while still smarting with disappointment, as though he could have prevented it. But he left without speaking, and his mother took his part.

“Don’t treat the poor boy harshly, Vincy. He’ll do well yet, although that wicked man deceived him. As surely as I’m sitting here, Fred will turn out well. Why else was he saved from the edge of the grave? I call it robbery. Promising him the land was as good as giving it. And what counts as a promise if making everybody believe you doesn’t? Besides, he actually left him ten thousand pounds and then withdrew it.”
“Withdrew it!” Mr. Vincy repeated irritably. “The boy brings bad luck, Lucy, that’s what I say. And you’ve always indulged him.”
“He was my first, Vincy. You made quite a fuss over him yourself when he arrived. Nobody could have been prouder,” said Mrs. Vincy, readily regaining her cheerful smile.
“Who can tell what a baby will grow into? No doubt I behaved like a fool,” her husband said, though his voice had softened.

“But whose children are handsomer or better than ours? Fred is miles ahead of other people’s sons. You can hear in the way he speaks that he’s mixed with university men. And where would you find another girl like Rosamond? Put her beside the grandest lady in the country and the comparison would only flatter her. Look at Mr. Lydgate. He’s been everywhere and mixed with the best society, and he fell in love with her straightaway. Not that I wouldn’t have preferred Rosamond to wait before getting engaged. On a visit she might have met someone who’d have been a much better match—I mean visiting her schoolfriend Miss Willoughby. That family has relations every bit as grand as Mr. Lydgate’s.”
“Damn their relations!” exclaimed Mr. Vincy. “I’ve had my fill of relations. I don’t want a son-in-law whose only recommendation is his family.”

“But, my dear,” Mrs. Vincy replied, “you seemed perfectly delighted. I wasn’t home, admittedly, but Rosamond said you’d raised no objection whatever to the engagement. She’s already started buying the finest linen and cambric for her underclothes.”

“Not with my approval,” said Mr. Vincy. “I’ve enough on my hands this year with an idle rascal for a son, without buying wedding clothes as well. Money couldn’t be tighter; everyone’s being ruined. I doubt Lydgate possesses a farthing. I won’t consent to the wedding. They can wait, as their elders did before them.”
“Rosamond will be very upset, Vincy. You know you’ve never been able to bear refusing her.”
“Yes, I have. The sooner they break it off, the better. At this rate he’ll never earn a living. All I hear of him making is enemies.”
“But Mr. Bulstrode thinks very highly of him, my dear. I’d expect the marriage to please _him_.”

“The devil it would!” said Mr. Vincy. “Bulstrode won’t support them. If Lydgate imagines I’m providing money to set up their house, he’s mistaken. That’s all. I shall probably have to give up my horses soon. You’d better pass that on to Rosy.”

Mr. Vincy often followed this course: agree rashly in a jovial mood, then, on realizing his rashness, get someone else to perform the unpleasant retraction. Mrs. Vincy, never willingly opposing her husband, told Rosamond what he had said first thing next morning. Rosamond listened silently while examining some worked muslin. At the end she turned her graceful neck in a particular way which only long acquaintance would have taught you signified absolute obstinacy.
“What do you think, darling?” her mother asked with affectionate respect.

“Papa means no such thing,” Rosamond answered with complete composure. “He has always wanted me to marry the man I love. I intend to marry Mr. Lydgate. Papa gave his consent seven weeks ago. And I hope we’ll take Mrs. Bretton’s house.”

“Well, my dear, I’ll leave your papa to you. You always manage everyone. But whenever we buy the damask, we must go to Sadler’s—much better than Hopkins’s. Mrs. Bretton’s house is very big, though. I’d love you to have it, but furnishing it will be expensive: carpets and everything else, besides silver and glass. And you’ve heard your papa says he’ll give no money. Do you suppose Mr. Lydgate is counting on any?”
“Surely you don’t imagine I could ask him, Mamma. Naturally he knows his own circumstances.”

“He may have expected money, though, my dear. We all thought you’d receive a nice legacy too, besides Fred’s. Now everything is so dreadful. There’s no pleasure in thinking about anything, with that poor boy so disappointed.”

“That doesn’t concern my marriage, Mamma. Fred needs to stop being idle. I’m taking this upstairs to Miss Morgan; she’s very good at open hemming. Mary Garth could do some sewing for me now, I should think. Her needlework is exquisite—it’s the nicest thing about her. I’d love double hems on all my cambric frills, and they take such a long time.”

Mrs. Vincy was right to trust Rosamond’s ability to manage her father. For all his bluster, Mr. Vincy got his own way outside his dinners and his coursing about as rarely as a prime minister. Circumstances easily overpowered him, as they do most pleasure-loving, red-faced men. The circumstance called Rosamond was especially powerful, thanks to that gentle persistence which, as we know, lets a soft white living thing force its way through opposing rock. Papa was no rock. His only consistency lay in recurring changes of impulse, sometimes called habit. These gave him little chance of taking the one decisive course over his daughter’s engagement: investigating Lydgate’s finances thoroughly, declaring that he himself could provide no money, and forbidding either a hasty wedding or an engagement that would have to last too long. Written down, that sounds simple and easy. But an unpleasant resolution formed in the cold morning had as many enemies as an early frost and rarely survived the day’s warming influences. Even Mr. Vincy’s usual indirect but emphatic ways of expressing disapproval were much restricted here. Lydgate’s pride made insinuations plainly dangerous, and throwing his hat on the floor was impossible. Mr. Vincy was slightly awed by him; slightly vain that he wanted Rosamond; slightly reluctant to discuss money, since his own position was weak; slightly afraid of losing an argument to a better-educated, better-bred man; and slightly afraid of displeasing his daughter. The role he preferred was generous host, beyond criticism. Business prevented any formal announcement of opposition during the first half of the day. Dinner, wine, whist, and general contentment prevented it during the second. Meanwhile each passing hour left its little deposit, gradually building the final reason for inaction: it was too late to act. The accepted suitor spent most evenings at Lowick Gate. Under Mr. Vincy’s eyes, courtship flourished without depending in the least on advances from fathers-in-law or anticipated professional earnings. Young love spins such a delicate web! Even its anchors, the things from which its fine threads hang, are barely visible: fingertips briefly touching, glances meeting from blue and dark eyes, unfinished sentences, tiny movements of cheek and lip, the faintest tremors. The web itself consists of beliefs that arise unbidden, indefinable joys, one life reaching toward another, visions of wholeness, limitless trust. Lydgate spun it out of himself at astonishing speed, despite experience supposedly completed by the drama of Laure, and despite medicine and biology too. Examining softened muscle, or eyes displayed on a dish like Santa Lucia’s, and other incidents of scientific research appear less incompatible with poetic love than natural dullness or a lively devotion to the coarsest prose of life. Rosamond, meanwhile, was like a water lily opening in amazement at its own fuller existence. She, too, worked busily at their shared web. This all happened in the drawing-room corner by the piano. However fine its threads, the light turned them into a rainbow visible to many besides Mr. Farebrother. Without a formal announcement, everyone in Middlemarch became certain that Miss Vincy and Mr. Lydgate were engaged.
Aunt Bulstrode grew anxious again. This time she approached her brother, deliberately visiting him at the warehouse to avoid Mrs. Vincy’s changeableness. His answers did not reassure her.

“Walter, surely you haven’t let all this proceed without investigating Mr. Lydgate’s prospects?” Mrs. Bulstrode’s eyes widened solemnly as she looked at her brother, in his irritable warehouse mood. “Think how this girl has been raised—in luxury and, I’m sorry to say, far too much worldliness. How will she manage on little money?”

“Confound it, Harriet! What am I to do when men settle here without being asked by me? Did you close your door to Lydgate? Nobody has promoted him more than Bulstrode. I never made a fuss over the fellow. Go and discuss it with your husband instead of me.”
“Really, Walter, how can this be Mr. Bulstrode’s fault? He certainly never wanted the engagement.”
“If Bulstrode hadn’t supported him, I would never have invited him.”
“But you brought him in to treat Fred, and that surely was a mercy,” Mrs. Bulstrode said, losing her way in the argument’s complications.

“Mercy, I don’t know,” said Mr. Vincy sharply. “What I know is my family causes me more worry than I care for. I was a good brother to you before you married Bulstrode, Harriet. He doesn’t always show your family the friendliness one might reasonably expect.” Mr. Vincy resembled a Jesuit very little, yet the most skillful Jesuit could scarcely have redirected a question more neatly. Harriet now had to defend her husband instead of reproaching her brother. The conversation wandered so far from its starting point that it ended with a recent clash between the brothers-in-law at a parish meeting.

Mrs. Bulstrode kept her brother’s complaints from her husband, but that evening she mentioned Rosamond and Lydgate. He did not share her affectionate concern. He spoke only with resignation about the hazards of starting a medical practice and the need for caution.
“Surely we ought to pray for that thoughtless girl, brought up as she has been,” Mrs. Bulstrode said, hoping to stir his feelings.

“Indeed, my dear,” Mr. Bulstrode agreed. “Those who do not belong to this world can do little else to check the mistakes of people stubbornly devoted to it. We must learn to accept that where your brother’s family is concerned. I should have preferred Mr. Lydgate not to make such a marriage. But my association with him extends only to employing his abilities for God’s purposes, in accordance with the example of divine government under every dispensation.”

Mrs. Bulstrode let the matter drop. She attributed her slight dissatisfaction to her own deficient spirituality. She believed her husband belonged among the men whose memoirs ought to be written after their deaths.

Lydgate himself, once accepted, was ready to accept every consequence, all of which he believed he could foresee perfectly. Naturally he must marry within a year—perhaps six months. He had not planned this, but his other plans would not be obstructed: they would merely rearrange themselves. Marriage naturally called for the usual preparations. He would need a house instead of his present rooms. Having heard Rosamond admire old Mrs. Bretton’s house in Lowick Gate, he noticed when her death left it empty and immediately began negotiating for it.

He did this as a minor matter, much as he ordered everything necessary for perfect dress from his tailor, without imagining he was extravagant. Indeed, he would have despised a display of expense. His work had acquainted him with every degree of poverty, and he felt deeply for those suffering hardship. He would have behaved impeccably at a table where sauce came in a jug with a broken handle. Of a grand dinner, he might remember only a man who had talked well. Yet it had never occurred to him to live otherwise than in what he would have called the ordinary way, with green glasses for hock and excellent service at meals. He had warmed himself at French social theories without carrying away any scent of singeing. We can handle even the most radical opinions unharmed while our furniture, dinner parties, and preference for a personal coat of arms bind us inseparably to the established order. Lydgate did not, in any case, incline toward radical opinions. Particular about his boots, he would have disliked barefoot doctrines. Only in medical reform and the pursuit of discovery was he radical. Elsewhere in practical life he followed inherited habits, partly from the personal pride and unthinking self-centeredness I have already called commonness, partly from the innocence that comes of absorption in favorite ideas.

When Lydgate privately considered the consequences of the engagement that had crept up on him, he worried about too little time, not too little money. Being in love, and constantly expected by someone who always proved prettier than memory could make her, certainly interfered with diligent use of spare hours. Some “plodding German fellow” might use those hours to make the great discovery now so close at hand. This was actually an argument against postponing marriage too long, as Lydgate suggested one day to Mr. Farebrother. The Vicar had brought some pond specimens to examine under a better microscope than his own. Finding Lydgate’s table of instruments and specimens in disorder, he remarked sarcastically—
“Eros has gone downhill. He began by bringing order and harmony; now he’s restoring chaos.”
“At certain stages, yes,” said Lydgate, smiling and raising his eyebrows as he adjusted the microscope. “A better order follows afterward.”
“Before long?” the Vicar asked.

“I certainly hope so. This unsettled situation eats up time, and for a man with scientific ideas, every moment offers a chance. I’m convinced marriage is best for anyone wanting to work consistently. Then everything is at home. No distracting questions about his personal future; he can have peace and freedom.”
“Lucky devil,” said the Vicar, “to have all that ahead of you—Rosamond, peace, and freedom, all yours. And here I am with only a pipe and microscopic pond creatures. Well, are you ready?”

Lydgate did not tell the Vicar his other reason for wanting a shorter courtship. Even with love intoxicating him, it irritated him to spend so much time among the Vincys, obliged to join in Middlemarch gossip, lengthy festivities, whist, and general pointlessness. He had to listen respectfully when Mr. Vincy settled questions with decisive ignorance, especially the question of which drinks best pickled one’s insides against unhealthy air. Mrs. Vincy’s simple openness carried no suspicion that she might subtly offend her prospective son-in-law’s taste. Altogether, Lydgate had to admit he was marrying slightly beneath him in Rosamond’s family. But that exquisite creature suffered in much the same way herself. At least he could take pleasure in knowing that marriage to him would give her a much-needed change of soil.
“Darling!” he said one evening, very gently, sitting beside her and studying her face—

First, however, I must mention that he had found her alone in the drawing room. The great old-fashioned window, nearly as wide as the room, stood open to the summer fragrance from the back garden. Her parents had gone to a party; everyone else was outside with the butterflies.
“Darling! Your eyes are red.”
“Are they?” Rosamond replied. “I wonder what caused that.” She was not one to pour out complaints or wishes. Those emerged gracefully only when invited.
“You can’t hide it from me!” Lydgate said, tenderly covering both her hands with his. “Isn’t there a little tear on that eyelash? Something upsets you, and you keep it from me. That’s not loving.”
“Why tell you things you can’t change? They’re ordinary everyday troubles. Perhaps they’ve been a little worse recently.”
“Trouble with your family. Don’t hesitate to tell me. I can guess.”

“Papa has been particularly irritable. Fred angers him. They had another quarrel this morning, because Fred threatens to waste his entire education and take up something quite beneath him. And then there’s—”

Rosamond paused, her cheeks beginning to color. Lydgate had not seen her distressed since the morning they became engaged. Never had he felt more passionately for her than now. He gently kissed her hesitant lips as if to help them speak.
“I think Papa isn’t entirely pleased with our engagement,” Rosamond went on, almost whispering. “Last night he said he’d certainly speak to you and insist on its being broken off.”
“Would you break it off?” Lydgate demanded, suddenly forceful, almost angry.
“I never abandon anything I’ve decided to do,” Rosamond replied. Touching this subject restored her composure.
“God bless you!” Lydgate kissed her again. Such firmness of purpose, properly directed, was adorable. He continued—
“Your father’s too late to insist we give each other up. You’re of age, and I claim you. If anyone makes you unhappy, that only gives us a reason to marry sooner.”

The blue eyes meeting his glowed with unmistakable joy. Their radiance seemed to bathe his entire future in gentle sunshine. Perfect happiness appeared to be only a few weeks away, more or less: the sort known in the Arabian Nights, when one steps out of a street’s labor and quarrels into a paradise where everything is bestowed and nothing demanded.
“Why wait?” he urged passionately. “I’ve taken the house. We can soon arrange everything else, can’t we? You won’t worry about new clothes. We can buy those later.”

“You clever men do have extraordinary ideas!” Rosamond’s dimples deepened as she laughed more freely than usual at this comical reversal. “I’ve never heard of buying wedding clothes after the wedding.”

“Surely you wouldn’t make me wait months just for clothes?” said Lydgate. He half believed she was playfully tormenting him, and half feared she truly hesitated to marry soon. “Think what greater happiness we have ahead, even compared with this: always together, free of other people, arranging our lives to suit ourselves. Tell me, darling, how soon can you belong to me altogether?”

His appeal was serious, as though any fanciful delay would do him an injury. Rosamond grew serious too, and thoughtful. In fact, she was working through the complications of lace edging, stockings, and petticoat tucks in order to offer an approximate answer.
“Six weeks would be plenty. Say it would, Rosamond,” Lydgate urged, releasing her hands and gently putting an arm around her.
One small hand immediately rose to smooth her hair. She tilted her neck thoughtfully, then said in a serious tone—
“We’d need to arrange the household linen and furniture. Still, Mamma could supervise those while we’re away.”
“Certainly. We must take a week or so away.”

“Oh, longer than that!” Rosamond said earnestly. She was thinking about evening dresses for visiting Sir Godwin Lydgate. For a long time she had secretly hoped to spend at least a delightful quarter of her honeymoon there, even if she postponed meeting the uncle who was a doctor of divinity—a pleasing, though quieter, distinction too, when supported by good birth. Her look expressed wondering protest. Lydgate readily assumed she wished to prolong their sweet solitude together.
“Anything you wish, darling, once we’ve settled the date. But let’s make a firm decision and end whatever unhappiness you’re experiencing. Six weeks! I’m certain that’s enough.”

“I could certainly hurry the sewing,” Rosamond replied. “Then will you speak to Papa? Writing to him might be better.” She blushed and looked at him as garden flowers seem to look at us when we walk happily among them in the surpassing evening light. Is there not a soul beyond words, half child, half nymph, in those delicate petals glowing and breathing around their deeply colored centers?

His lips brushed her ear and the little curve of neck beneath it. They sat motionless for many minutes, which flowed past like a softly bubbling stream kissed by sunlight. Rosamond believed nobody could be more in love. Lydgate believed that, after all his reckless mistakes and ridiculous gullibility, he had found perfect womanhood. He could almost feel already the exquisite marital affection of an accomplished creature who revered his lofty thinking and important work and would never disturb them. Quietly, as if by magic, she would keep the house and accounts in order, yet always have her fingers ready for the lute, transforming life into romance at a touch. Her education reached exactly the proper feminine boundary, not a hair beyond it. Therefore she would be compliant and ready to obey instructions reaching her from that boundary. More than ever he saw that his plan to remain a bachelor much longer had been mistaken. Marriage would help rather than hinder him. The next day, accompanying a patient to Brassing, he happened to see a dinner service that seemed exactly right and bought it on the spot. Attending to such things when they occurred to you saved time, and he hated ugly crockery. The service was costly, but perhaps that was simply the nature of dinner services. Furnishing a home inevitably cost money; still, it needed doing only once.
“It sounds lovely,” Mrs. Vincy said when Lydgate described his purchase. “Exactly what Rosy should have. Heaven grant it doesn’t get broken!”

“One must engage servants who don’t break things,” Lydgate replied. Certainly his reasoning rested on an incomplete view of consequences. But at that time scarcely any kind of reasoning lacked some endorsement from scientific men.

There was naturally no need to delay telling Mamma anything. She rarely adopted an unhappy view, and, being happily married herself, felt almost nothing but pride at her daughter’s marriage. Rosamond nevertheless had sound reasons for advising Lydgate to approach Papa in writing. To prepare him for the letter, she walked with him to the warehouse next morning and told him on the way that Mr. Lydgate wanted an early wedding.

“Nonsense, darling!” Mr. Vincy replied. “What money has he to marry on? You’d be far better off ending the engagement. I’ve already told you that plainly enough. Why give you such an education if you’re going to marry a poor man? It’s cruel for a father to witness.”
“He isn’t poor, Papa. He purchased Mr. Peacock’s practice, which is said to bring in eight or nine hundred a year.”
“Rubbish! What does buying a practice amount to? He might as well purchase next year’s swallows. It’ll slide straight through his hands.”
“Quite the reverse, Papa. He’ll expand it. Look how the Chettams and Casaubons have called him in.”
“I hope he understands he’ll get nothing from me. After this disappointment over Fred, and with Parliament about to be dissolved, machines being smashed everywhere, an election approaching—”
“Dear Papa! How does any of that concern my wedding?”

“A great deal! We could all be ruined, for all I know, with the country in this condition! People call it the end of the world; be hanged if it doesn’t look like it! Anyway, this is no time to take money out of my business. I’d like Lydgate to understand that.”
“I’m certain he expects nothing, Papa. His connections are so distinguished that he’s bound to advance somehow. He’s working on scientific discoveries.”
Her father said nothing.

“I can’t abandon my one chance of happiness, Papa. Mr. Lydgate is a gentleman. I could never love anyone who wasn’t a gentleman in every way. You wouldn’t want me to fall into a decline, as Arabella Hawley did. Besides, you know I never alter my decisions.”
Still her father did not answer.
“Promise you’ll agree to our wishes, Papa. We’ll never give each other up, and you’ve always disapproved of long engagements and marrying late.”
After a little more coaxing in this vein, Mr. Vincy said, “Well, well, child. He must write to me before I can reply.” Rosamond knew she had won.

Mr. Vincy’s reply chiefly required Lydgate to insure his life, which he immediately agreed to do. The idea was wonderfully reassuring if Lydgate died, though meanwhile it supplied no means of living. Nevertheless, it seemed to settle everyone’s anxieties about Rosamond’s wedding. The necessary shopping went ahead enthusiastically, but not without due economy. A bride intending to visit a baronet must possess a few superb handkerchiefs. Beyond the six absolutely indispensable ones, however, Rosamond was content with something less than the finest embroidery and Valenciennes lace. Lydgate, too, discovering how much his eight hundred pounds had shrunk since his arrival in Middlemarch, resisted some old-pattern silver shown to him at Kibble’s in Brassing, where he went for forks and spoons. He was too proud to behave as if he expected Mr. Vincy to advance money for furniture. Everything need not be paid for immediately, so some bills would remain outstanding; but he wasted no time guessing what dowry his father-in-law might provide to help settle them. He intended no extravagance. Necessary things had to be purchased, and buying inferior quality would be false economy. Such matters were incidental. He expected science and his profession to be the sole objects of his passionate effort, but could not imagine pursuing them in a home like Wrench’s, with every door open, worn oilcloth, children in dirty pinafores, and lunch lingering as bones, black-handled knives, and willow-pattern plates. Then again, Wrench had a miserable, sluggish wife who wrapped herself indoors like a mummy in a large shawl. His domestic arrangements must have been badly chosen from the start.
Rosamond, for her part, did plenty of speculating, although her quick ability to perceive and imitate proper behavior warned her not to reveal it too bluntly.
“I’d so love to meet your family,” she said one day as they discussed the wedding journey. “Perhaps we could choose a route that lets us visit them on the way home. Which uncle is your favorite?”
“Oh, Godwin, I suppose. He’s a kindly old fellow.”
“You spent a great deal of time at his house in Quallingham as a boy, didn’t you? I’d love to see the place and everything you knew then. Have you told him you’re getting married?”
“No,” Lydgate answered casually, turning in his chair and rumpling his hair.

“Then tell him, you naughty, neglectful nephew. Perhaps he’ll invite you to bring me to Quallingham. You could show me the grounds, and I could picture you there as a boy. Remember, you see my home exactly as it’s been since my childhood. It isn’t fair that I know so little of yours. Unless perhaps you’d be a little ashamed of me—I hadn’t thought of that.”

Lydgate smiled tenderly. He genuinely accepted her suggestion that the proud delight of displaying such a charming bride merited a little effort. Now that he considered it, he would enjoy revisiting the old places with Rosamond.
“All right, I’ll write. My cousins are dreadful bores, though.”
To Rosamond, the ability to dismiss a baronet’s family so lightly seemed magnificent. She felt very satisfied at the prospect of judging them contemptuously for herself.
A day or two later, however, Mamma nearly spoiled everything by remarking—
“I do hope your uncle Sir Godwin won’t think Rosy beneath him, Mr. Lydgate. I should expect a handsome present from him. A thousand or two must be nothing to a baronet.”

“Mamma!” Rosamond blushed deeply. Lydgate felt so sorry for her that he said nothing and went to the far end of the room to study a print with apparent absorption, as if his attention had wandered. Mamma received a little lecture from her daughter afterward and was as compliant as usual. Rosamond reflected, however, that any visit to Middlemarch by those tiresome, well-born cousins would expose them to much in her own family that might shock them. It therefore seemed desirable for Lydgate eventually to secure a distinguished position somewhere else. Surely that would not be difficult for a man who could make discoveries and had a titled uncle. Lydgate, you see, had spoken ardently to Rosamond about his hopes for the highest purposes of his life. He had delighted in being heard by a creature who would support him with the sweetness of satisfying affection, beauty, and rest—the kind of help our thoughts receive from a summer sky and meadows bordered with flowers.

Lydgate put great faith in the psychological distinction between what, for variety’s sake, I shall call goose and gander. Above all, he trusted the goose’s inborn submissiveness to complement so beautifully the gander’s strength.

chapters.title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXVII
paragraphs:
Thrice happy she that is so well assured
Unto herself and settled so in heart
That neither will for better be allured
Ne fears to worse with any chance to start,
But like a steddy ship doth strongly part
The raging waves and keeps her course aright;
Ne aught for tempest doth from it depart,
Ne aught for fairer weather’s false delight.
Such self-assurance need not fear the spight
Of grudging foes; ne favour seek of friends;
But in the stay of her own stedfast might
Neither to one herself nor other bends.
Most happy she that most assured doth rest,
But he most happy who such one loves best.
—SPENSER.

Mr. Vincy’s uncertainty about whether a general election or the end of the world was approaching only faintly represented the confusion of provincial opinion. George IV was dead, Parliament dissolved, Wellington and Peel widely disparaged, and the new King apologetic. By the glowworm light available in country towns, how could people distinguish their own thoughts amid it all? A Tory government was passing Liberal measures; Tory peers and voters wanted to elect Liberals rather than supporters of ministers they considered traitors. Demands for remedies seemed mysteriously remote from private interests, and became suspect when disagreeable neighbors supported them. Middlemarch newspaper buyers occupied a peculiar position. During the agitation over the Catholic Question, many had stopped buying the “Pioneer,” a paper bearing a motto from Charles James Fox and marching at the head of progress. It had sided with Peel on the Catholics, staining its Liberalism by tolerating Jesuitry and Baal. Yet the “Trumpet” did not satisfy them either. After its blasts against Rome, and amid a general limpness of public opinion, when nobody knew who would support whom, its notes had grown feeble.

According to a notable article in the “Pioneer,” the country’s urgent needs might now properly overcome any reluctance to enter public life in men whose long experience had given their minds breadth as well as concentration, firm judgment as well as tolerance, dispassion as well as energy. In other words, all those qualities which humanity’s melancholy experience finds least willing to live together.

Mr. Hackbutt’s fluent conversation was circulating more widely than usual just then, with considerable uncertainty about where it would finally flow. In Mr. Hawley’s office he was heard to declare that the article “emanated” from Brooke of Tipton, who had secretly purchased the “Pioneer” several months earlier.

“Trouble brewing, then?” said Mr. Hawley. “After drifting about like a stray tortoise, he’s taken it into his head to become popular. The worse for him. I’ve been watching him for some time. We’ll give him a thorough ducking. He’s a damned bad landlord. What’s an old county gentleman doing courting a vulgar set of dark-blue freemen? As for his newspaper, I only hope he’ll write it himself. We could afford to pay him for that.”

“I’m told he’s hired a remarkably brilliant young man as editor, someone capable of writing leading articles in the finest style, equal to anything in the London papers. And he intends to take a very elevated line on Reform.”
“Let Brooke reform his rent roll. He’s a damned old miser, and every building on his estate is falling apart. I suppose this young fellow is some disreputable London adventurer.”
“His name is Ladislaw. They say he’s of foreign descent.”
“I recognize the breed,” Mr. Hawley replied. “Some sort of agent. He’ll start by flourishing the Rights of Man and finish by murdering a girl. That’s their way.”

“You must admit there are abuses, Hawley,” said Mr. Hackbutt, anticipating a political disagreement with his family lawyer. “I’d never support extreme opinions. My own position is Huskisson’s, in fact. But I can’t ignore the consideration that large towns without representation—”

“Damn the large towns!” Mr. Hawley had no patience for exposition. “I know rather too much about Middlemarch elections. Abolish every pocket borough tomorrow and enfranchise every mushroom town in the kingdom; all you’ll do is make getting into Parliament more expensive. I rely on facts.”

Mr. Hawley resented both the idea of an agent editing the “Pioneer” and Brooke’s entry into active politics, as though a tortoise of wandering interests had thrust out its little head in ambition and reared up. Yet some of Mr. Brooke’s family resented it still more. The truth had gradually leaked out, like the discovery that your neighbor has established an offensive manufacture whose odors you must permanently endure without legal recourse. The “Pioneer” had been bought secretly before Will Ladislaw arrived. The awaited opportunity came when its owner proved willing to part with valuable property that yielded no profit. In the time since Mr. Brooke had written his invitation to Will, the germ of an ambition to bring his mind to bear on the wider world had been growing in secret. It had existed since his youth, but until now something had always impeded it.

His pleasure in his guest, greater even than expected, did much to encourage this growth. Will not only knew his way around all those artistic and literary subjects Mr. Brooke had once explored. He was also extraordinarily quick at grasping the political situation and treating it in the broad-minded spirit which, when supported by a good memory, lends itself to apt quotation and an effective handling of the whole.

“He strikes me as a sort of Shelley, you know,” Mr. Brooke took an opportunity to tell Mr. Casaubon, intending to please him. “Nothing objectionable, I don’t mean—loose morals, atheism, any of that, you know. I’m certain Ladislaw’s feelings are sound in every respect. We talked a great deal last night, as it happens. But he has that same enthusiasm for liberty, freedom, emancipation. Excellent things when guided—properly guided, you know. I think I can set him on the right course. And it’s especially gratifying that he’s your relative, Casaubon.”

If “the right course” meant anything more definite than the rest of this speech, Mr. Casaubon silently hoped it meant employment a long way from Lowick. He had disliked Will while supporting him, and disliked him still more now that Will had refused support. So it goes with those of us whose disposition contains an uneasy jealousy. If our own talents chiefly involve burrowing, we suspect that our honey-sipping cousin, against whom we have serious objections, secretly despises us. Anyone admiring him indirectly criticizes us. Our scrupulous sense of right keeps us above the meanness of harming him. Instead, we actively confer benefits to satisfy every claim he has on us. Writing him checks establishes a superiority he must acknowledge, and this softens our bitterness. Now, abruptly and capriciously, Mr. Casaubon had lost that superiority, except as a memory. His hostility toward Will arose from something deeper than an aging husband’s ordinary jealousy. It had grown out of lifelong pretensions and dissatisfactions. But Dorothea’s presence—Dorothea as a young wife who had herself shown an offensive capacity for criticism—inevitably focused an uneasiness that had once been diffuse.

Will Ladislaw, meanwhile, felt his dislike growing at gratitude’s expense, and argued extensively with himself to justify it. Casaubon hated him; he knew that perfectly. The instant he entered, he could detect bitterness around the mouth and venom in the glance, enough almost to justify open war despite past kindness. He owed Casaubon much for the past, but really, marrying this particular wife canceled the debt. Ought gratitude for kindness to oneself to outweigh anger at a wrong done to someone else? Casaubon had wronged Dorothea by marrying her. A man had a duty to know himself better. If he chose to grow gray gnawing bones in a cave, he had no right to entice a girl into sharing it. “The most horrible sacrifice of a virgin,” Will called it. He pictured Dorothea’s secret suffering as though composing a lament for a tragic chorus. But he would never lose sight of her. He would protect her; if he sacrificed everything else, he would still protect her. She should know she had one slave in the world. Will possessed what Sir Thomas Browne called a “passionate prodigality” in his declarations, to himself as well as to others. The plain truth was that nothing attracted him then so powerfully as Dorothea’s presence.

Formal invitations had been absent, however: Will had never been asked to Lowick. Mr. Brooke, sure he was doing all the agreeable things poor, absorbed Casaubon forgot to do, had arranged several times to bring Ladislaw there. Meanwhile he introduced him everywhere else whenever possible as “a young relative of Casaubon’s.” Will had not seen Dorothea alone. Even so, their meetings restored her old sense of youthful companionship with someone cleverer than herself who nevertheless seemed willing to be influenced by her. Before marriage, poor Dorothea had seldom found much space in other people’s minds for what she most wanted to say. And her husband’s superior instruction, as we know, had brought her less pleasure than expected. When she spoke to Mr. Casaubon with eager interest, he listened patiently, as though she were quoting an elementary Delectus passage he had known since childhood. Sometimes he curtly named ancient sects or individuals who had held similar ideas, implying an excessive supply of that commodity already. Sometimes he told her she was mistaken and repeated the assertion her remark had challenged.

Will Ladislaw, however, always appeared to discover more in her words than she did herself. Dorothea had little vanity, but she had a passionate woman’s need to exercise a kindly influence by making another soul happy. The mere possibility of seeing Will now and then was therefore like a little window opened in her prison wall, offering a glimpse of sunlit air. That pleasure began to overcome her first alarm about what her husband might think of Will’s arrival as her uncle’s guest. Mr. Casaubon had said nothing on that subject.

Will wanted a private conversation with Dorothea and grew impatient with circumstances moving so slowly. Dante and Beatrice, Petrarch and Laura, might have enjoyed little earthly conversation, but time changes the proportions of things. In later ages fewer sonnets and more conversation are preferable. Necessity justified a scheme, though fear of offending Dorothea limited his ingenuity. At last he discovered a wish to sketch a particular view at Lowick. One morning, when Mr. Brooke had to take the Lowick road toward the county town, Will asked to be dropped there with sketchbook and folding stool. Without announcing himself at the manor, he chose a drawing position from which he must see Dorothea if she came out. He knew she generally walked for an hour each morning.

The weather defeated his plan. Clouds assembled with treacherous speed, rain fell, and Will had to shelter in the house. Relying on his family connection, he meant to go into the drawing room and wait without being announced. Seeing his old acquaintance, the butler, in the hall, he said, “Don’t announce me, Pratt. I’ll wait until lunch. I know Mr. Casaubon dislikes being interrupted in the library.”

“The master’s out, sir. Only Mrs. Casaubon’s in the library. I’d better let her know you’ve come.” Pratt was a red-cheeked man who enjoyed lively chats with Tantripp and often agreed that Madam must find life dull.
“Oh, all right. This wretched rain has stopped me drawing,” Will replied. He was so happy that pretending indifference came delightfully easily.
A minute later he stood in the library, and Dorothea greeted him with her sweet, unaffected smile.

“Mr. Casaubon has gone to the Archdeacon’s,” she said immediately. “I’m not sure he’ll return much before dinner. He didn’t know how long he’d be away. Did you need to discuss something particular with him?”
“No, I came to draw, but the rain drove me indoors. Otherwise I wouldn’t have interrupted you yet. I thought Mr. Casaubon was here, and I know he dislikes interruptions at this time of day.”
“Then I owe the rain a debt. I’m so pleased to see you.” These ordinary words had the unguarded sincerity of an unhappy schoolchild receiving a visitor.

“Actually, I came hoping to see you alone,” Will admitted, mysteriously compelled to match her simplicity. He could not stop to ask himself why he should not. “I wanted us to talk as we did in Rome. Having other people present always changes things.”

“Yes,” Dorothea agreed in her clear, full voice. “Please sit down.” She sat on a dark ottoman against a background of brown books. In her plain dress of thin white wool, wearing no ornament except her wedding ring, she seemed vowed to be unlike all other women. Will sat opposite, two yards away. Light fell on his bright curls and fine, slightly petulant profile, with its defiant curves of chin and lip. They looked at each other like two flowers that had opened just then and there. For the moment Dorothea forgot her husband’s inexplicable irritation with Will. To speak without fear to the one person she had found receptive was fresh water to thirsty lips. Looking backward through unhappiness, she magnified a former comfort.
“I’ve often wished we could talk again,” she said at once. “It’s strange to remember how much I told you.”

“I remember every word,” Will replied. His soul held an inexpressible contentment at being with someone worthy of perfect love. I think his feelings then were perfect too. We mortals have divine moments, when love finds satisfaction in the completeness of the person loved.

“Since Rome, I’ve tried to learn a great deal,” Dorothea said. “I can read a little Latin, and I’m starting to understand a very little Greek. I’m more useful to Mr. Casaubon now. I can look up references and spare his eyes in various ways. But scholarship is terribly difficult. People seem to exhaust themselves on the journey toward great thoughts, and when they reach them they’re too tired to enjoy them.”

“Anyone capable of great thoughts generally catches up with them before becoming decrepit,” Will answered with uncontrollable quickness. Certain sensitivities made Dorothea as quick as he was, however. Seeing her expression change, he immediately added, “Still, it’s certainly true that even the finest minds sometimes strain themselves too far in developing their ideas.”

“You’re correcting me,” said Dorothea. “I didn’t put it well. I meant that people with great thoughts wear themselves out working them through. I used to feel for them even as a little girl. I always thought the best use I could make of my life would be to help someone doing great work, and lighten his burden.”

She had drifted into this piece of personal history without feeling she was revealing a secret. Yet nothing she had ever told Will illuminated her marriage so clearly. He refrained from shrugging. Denied that muscular release, his thoughts turned all the more irritably to beautiful lips kissing holy skulls and other hollow things enshrined by the Church. He also had to keep those thoughts out of his speech.

“But you could easily help too much,” he said, “and exhaust yourself. Aren’t you indoors too much? You’re already paler. A secretary would be better for Mr. Casaubon. He could easily find a man to do half his work. That would spare him more effectively, and leave you to help in less demanding ways.”

“How can you suggest that?” Dorothea protested earnestly. “Helping him with his work is my only happiness. What else could I do? There’s no useful work for me in Lowick. All I want is to help him more. Besides, he objects to a secretary. Please don’t suggest it again.”
“Certainly I won’t, now that I understand your feelings. But both Mr. Brooke and Sir James Chettam have said they wish he had one.”

“Yes, but they don’t understand. They want me to spend hours riding, redesign the garden, build conservatories, anything to fill my time. I thought you’d understand that the mind needs other things,” she added with some impatience. “And Mr. Casaubon can’t bear the subject of a secretary.”
“You can excuse my mistake,” Will replied. “He used to speak as if he looked forward to having one. In fact, he once suggested the position to me. But I proved—not suitable enough.”
Trying to find in this an explanation that excused her husband’s obvious aversion, Dorothea smiled playfully. “You weren’t a sufficiently steady worker.”

“No,” Will agreed, tossing his head back like a spirited horse. Then the old irritable demon urged him to pinch another piece from the fragile moth wings of poor Mr. Casaubon’s glory. “And I’ve since realized he doesn’t want anyone examining his work closely enough to know exactly what he’s doing. He’s too doubtful, too unsure of himself. I may be worth very little, but he dislikes me because I disagree with him.”

Will did intend always to behave generously. But tongues are little triggers, usually pulled before general intentions can be brought into play. It was unbearable to leave Dorothea without a fair explanation of Casaubon’s dislike. Once he had spoken, though, he worried a little about how she would take it.

Dorothea remained unexpectedly quiet. She did not respond with instant indignation as she had on a similar occasion in Rome. The reason lay deep. She had stopped fighting against seeing the facts and was learning to see them clearly. Looking steadily now at her husband’s failure, and still more at his possible awareness of it, she seemed to see the one path on which duty could become tenderness. She might have rebuked Will’s frankness more sharply had her husband’s dislike not already commended him to her mercy. Until she understood its grounds better, that dislike must seem harsh.

She did not answer immediately. After gazing down thoughtfully, she said with some earnestness, “Whatever his feelings, Mr. Casaubon has overcome them in his behavior toward you. That deserves admiration.”

“Yes, he has recognized what justice requires within a family. Disinheriting my grandmother for what they called a _mesalliance_ was disgraceful. The only charge against her husband was that he was a Polish refugee who earned a living by teaching.”
“I wish I knew her whole story!” Dorothea exclaimed. “How did she manage the change from wealth to poverty? I wonder whether she was happy with her husband! Can you tell me much about them?”

“Very little. My grandfather was a patriot, a clever man, spoke several languages, had musical ability, taught all sorts of things to earn his bread. They both died fairly young. And apart from what my mother told me, I knew little of my father. He inherited the musical gifts. I remember his slow walk, his long, thin hands. One day stays in my mind: he was lying ill, and I was desperately hungry, with only a little piece of bread.”

“How unlike my own life!” Dorothea said with intense interest, clasping her hands in her lap. “I’ve always had too much of everything. But explain it to me. Mr. Casaubon can’t have known about you then.”

“No. But my father contacted him, and that was the last day I went hungry. Father died soon afterward, and my mother and I were well provided for. Mr. Casaubon always specifically acknowledged a duty toward us because of the cruel injustice done to his mother’s sister. But you already know all this.”

Deep down, Will knew he wanted to impress something on Dorothea that was rather new even in his own account of events: Mr. Casaubon had only ever been paying a debt to him. Will was much too decent to feel comfortable with ingratitude. Once gratitude becomes an issue to reason over, however, many ways of escaping its bonds present themselves.

“No,” Dorothea replied. “Mr. Casaubon has never liked dwelling on his own good deeds.” She did not feel that her husband’s conduct had been diminished. But this conception of what justice had required him to do for Will took a powerful hold on her. After a pause she added, “He never told me he supported your mother. Is she alive?”

“No. She died in an accident—a fall—four years ago. Oddly enough, she had run away from her family too, though not because of her husband. She would tell me nothing about them except that she left to earn her own living. She went on the stage, in fact. She had dark eyes and tight curls and never seemed to grow older. So you see, I have rebellious blood on both sides.” Will ended with a bright smile at Dorothea. She was still gazing ahead with grave absorption, like a child watching her first play.

Then she smiled too. “That’s your excuse, I suppose, for your own rebelliousness—against Mr. Casaubon’s wishes, I mean. Remember, you haven’t followed the course he thought best for you. If he dislikes you—you mentioned dislike earlier—or rather, if he’s shown any unhappy feeling toward you, you must remember how sensitive the strain of study has made him. Perhaps,” she went on in a pleading voice, “my uncle hasn’t told you how seriously ill he was. Those of us who are well, who can bear things, would be petty to dwell on little offenses from people carrying such heavy troubles.”

“You show me a better way,” Will said. “I won’t complain about that again.” His gentleness came from an inexpressible satisfaction at recognizing something Dorothea barely knew herself: she was retreating into the distance of pure pity and loyalty toward her husband. Will was ready to worship that pity and loyalty if she would let him join her in expressing them. “I’ve certainly been difficult at times,” he continued. “But if I can help it, I’ll never again say or do anything you’d disapprove of.”

“That’s very kind,” Dorothea said, smiling openly again. “Then I’ll have a little kingdom where I can make laws. But I suppose you’ll soon leave and escape my rule. You’ll tire of the Grange before long.”

“That’s something I wanted to discuss with you—one reason I hoped to see you alone. Mr. Brooke has suggested I stay nearby. He’s bought a Middlemarch newspaper and wants me to run it and assist him in other matters.”
“Wouldn’t that mean giving up better prospects?” Dorothea asked.

“Possibly. But people have always criticized me for dreaming of prospects instead of settling to work. Here’s an actual offer. If you don’t want me to accept, I won’t. Otherwise I’d prefer staying in this part of the country to leaving. There’s nobody elsewhere I belong to.”
“I’d very much like you to stay,” Dorothea answered immediately, with the same ready simplicity she had shown in Rome. At that instant she could think of no possible reason not to say it.
“Then stay I _will_,” said Ladislaw, tossing back his head. He stood and walked toward the window as if checking whether the rain had stopped.

A moment later, however, Dorothea fell into a habit growing stronger every day: remembering that her husband felt differently. She blushed deeply, doubly embarrassed at having expressed a wish that might oppose his, and at needing to reveal that disagreement to Will. His turned back made it easier for her to speak—

“But my opinion hardly matters in a question like this. You should take Mr. Casaubon’s advice. I was thinking only of my feelings, which have nothing to do with the actual issue. It occurs to me now that he might find the proposal unwise. Could you wait and discuss it with him?”

“I can’t stay today,” Will said, inwardly scorched by the possibility of Mr. Casaubon’s arrival. “The rain has stopped entirely. I told Mr. Brooke not to collect me. I’d rather walk the five miles. I’ll cross Halsell Common and watch the light on the wet grass. I enjoy that.”

He hurried over to shake hands, desperately wanting to say, “Don’t mention this to Mr. Casaubon,” but unable to risk it. No, he could not say such a thing. Asking her to be less open and straightforward would be like breathing on crystal through which you wanted to see the light. There was also the other great fear: that he himself might lose his brightness in her eyes, and remain forever without it.

“I wish you could have stayed,” Dorothea said with a faint sadness, rising and offering her hand. She too had an unspoken thought. Will certainly ought to consult Mr. Casaubon’s wishes without delay, but urging him might seem too dictatorial.

They therefore said only goodbye. Will left across the fields to avoid any chance of meeting Mr. Casaubon’s carriage, which in fact did not reach the gate until four. That was an awkward time to return. It was too early to relieve his weariness with the moral support of dressing for dinner, yet too late to strip his mind of the day’s empty ceremonies and business and plunge properly into serious study. Usually at such times he settled into a library armchair, closed his eyes, and let Dorothea read the London papers aloud. Today he declined, saying he had already been subjected to too many public details. But when she asked about his tiredness, he answered more cheerfully than usual. Then, with the laborious formality that never left him, even without waistcoat or cravat, he added—

“Today I enjoyed meeting my old acquaintance Dr. Spanning, and receiving praise from someone himself deserving of praise. He spoke most generously of my recent treatise on the Egyptian Mysteries. Indeed, his terms were such that modesty prevents my repeating them.” As he said this last part, Mr. Casaubon leaned over the arm of his chair and bobbed his head, apparently finding a muscular release in place of the repetition propriety forbade.
“I’m so glad you had that pleasure,” Dorothea said, delighted that he seemed less weary than usual at this hour. “Before you returned, I’d been sorry you happened to be out today.”
“Why, my dear?” Mr. Casaubon asked, leaning back again.

“Mr. Ladislaw came. He told me about a proposal Uncle has made, and I’d like to hear what you think.” She felt this really did concern her husband. Inexperienced as she was, she vaguely sensed that the position offered to Will did not fit his family connections. Certainly Mr. Casaubon deserved to be consulted. He said nothing, merely bowing.
“You know how many plans dear Uncle has. Apparently he’s bought one of the Middlemarch newspapers. He’s asked Mr. Ladislaw to remain nearby and manage it, as well as help him in other ways.”
She watched her husband while speaking. At first he blinked, then closed his eyes as though resting them, while his lips tightened. After a short pause, she asked rather timidly, “What do you think?”

“Did Mr. Ladislaw visit expressly to seek my opinion?” Mr. Casaubon’s eyes opened narrowly, fixing her with a look as sharp as a knife. His question touched a point on which she truly felt uneasy. But her face merely grew more serious, and she did not look away.
“No,” she answered at once. “He didn’t say he had come for your opinion. But when he told me about the proposal, he naturally expected me to pass it on.”
Her husband gave no answer.

“I was afraid you might object. Still, someone with so much ability could be very useful to my uncle, and help him do good more effectively. Mr. Ladislaw wants settled employment. He says people have criticized him for not looking for it. He’d prefer to stay here because nobody cares for him anywhere else.”

Dorothea thought that last consideration would soften her husband. When he still said nothing, she returned to Dr. Spanning and breakfast at the Archdeacon’s. Those subjects, however, had lost their sunshine.
Without telling Dorothea, Mr. Casaubon sent the following letter next morning. It began “Dear Mr. Ladislaw,” although previously he had always written “Will”—

“Mrs. Casaubon tells me you have received a proposal which, by no excessive stretch of inference, you have entertained to some degree. It would entail your residing in this neighborhood in a capacity affecting my own position. Considered in the light of my legitimate feelings, that effect makes my objection natural and justified; considered in the light of my responsibilities, it makes stating that objection a duty. I therefore inform you at once that accepting this proposal would be highly offensive to me. No reasonable person acquainted with our relationship would, I believe, deny that I have some right of veto here. Your recent conduct has relegated that relationship to the past, but cannot erase its force as a determining antecedent. I do not propose to comment on anyone’s judgment. I need only remind you that social fitness and propriety should prevent a fairly close relation of mine from becoming conspicuous in this vicinity in a position not only greatly inferior to my own, but associated at best with the superficial learning of literary or political adventurers. In any event, should you proceed otherwise, you can no longer be received at my house.
