Still, she wished Sir James could know what she and her husband had said about Will Ladislaw’s moral claim to the property. Then, she thought, he would see as clearly as she did that her husband’s strange, indelicate condition sprang chiefly from his bitter resistance to that claim, and not simply from more intimate feelings that were harder to discuss. Admittedly, Dorothea also wanted this known for Will’s sake, since her friends seemed to regard him only as a recipient of Mr. Casaubon’s charity. Why compare him to an Italian carrying white mice? Those words of Mrs. Cadwallader’s seemed a mocking caricature sketched in darkness by a malicious imp.

At Lowick, Dorothea searched every desk and drawer, every place where her husband had kept private papers. She found nothing addressed specifically to her except the “Synoptical Tabulation,” probably the first of many intended instructions. In arranging this legacy of work for Dorothea, as in everything else, Mr. Casaubon had proceeded slowly and hesitantly. Planning how to pass on his work had oppressed him just as doing it had: he felt he was laboriously moving through something dark and obstructive. His doubts about Dorothea’s ability to arrange his materials were overcome only by his doubts about any other editor. Eventually, however, he had built himself a hope from Dorothea’s character. What she resolved to do, she could accomplish; and he readily pictured her laboring, bound by a promise, to build a tomb bearing his name. Not that Mr. Casaubon called the projected volumes a tomb: he called them the Key to all Mythologies. But the months overtook him and his plans fell behind. He had found time only to ask for the promise through which he hoped to maintain his cold grip on Dorothea’s life.

That grip had loosened. Had she bound herself by a promise made from the depths of pity, she could have undertaken work which her judgment quietly told her was useless—except as a sacred act of faithfulness, itself a supreme purpose. But now her judgment was no longer restrained by dutiful devotion. It had been stirred to action by the bitter discovery that secrecy and suspicion had concealed an estrangement within her marriage. The living, suffering man was no longer there to awaken her compassion. All that remained was the memory of painful submission to a husband whose thoughts had been less noble than she believed. His excessive demands on his own behalf had blinded even his meticulous concern for his reputation, defeating his own pride by shocking men with ordinary standards of honor. As for the property that represented their broken bond, she would gladly have surrendered it and kept only her own original fortune, secured to her at marriage, had ownership not brought duties she ought not to evade. Troubling questions about that property kept forcing themselves upon her. Hadn’t she been right to think half of it should go to Will Ladislaw? Yet wasn’t that act of justice now impossible? Mr. Casaubon had found a cruelly effective way to prevent it. Even while indignant with him, she recoiled from any action that looked like a triumphant circumvention of his wishes.

After gathering the business papers she wanted to study, she locked the desks and drawers again. They held no personal words for her, no sign that in her husband’s solitary brooding his heart had reached towards her with an explanation or apology. She returned to Freshitt feeling that his last harsh demand and final harmful assertion of power remained surrounded by unbroken silence.

Dorothea now tried to direct her thoughts to immediate duties. One of them was something other people were determined to remind her of. Lydgate had listened eagerly when she mentioned the living. At the first opportunity he returned to it, seeing a chance to make amends for the deciding vote he had once cast against his uneasy conscience. “Rather than tell you about Mr. Tyke,” he said, “I’d like to speak about another man—Mr. Farebrother, the Vicar of St. Botolph’s. His living brings in very little, barely enough to support him and his family. His mother, aunt and sister all live with him and depend on him. I believe they’re the reason he never married. I’ve never heard better preaching—such clear, natural eloquence. He could have followed old Latimer in the pulpit at St. Paul’s Cross. His conversation is equally good, whatever the subject: fresh, unpretentious and clear. I think he’s a remarkable man. He ought to have achieved more than he has.”
“Why hasn’t he?” asked Dorothea, whose interest now extended to everyone who had fallen short of their own intentions.

“That’s difficult to answer,” said Lydgate. “I’ve found myself that doing the right thing is extraordinarily hard: so many forces pull at you at once. Farebrother often suggests he chose the wrong profession. He needs a wider field than a poor clergyman has, and I suppose he lacks influential friends to help him advance. He’s very interested in natural history and various sciences, and struggles to fit those interests into his position. He has no money to spare—scarcely enough to live on—and that’s driven him to cards. Middlemarch is a great town for whist. He plays for money, certainly, and wins quite a lot. Naturally, that draws him into company somewhat beneath him and makes him careless about certain things. Yet taking him altogether, despite that, I think he’s one of the least blameworthy men I’ve known. There’s no malice or duplicity in him, and those qualities often accompany a more respectable exterior.”
“I wonder whether the habit troubles his conscience,” Dorothea said. “I wonder whether he wishes he could give it up.”
“I’m sure he’d abandon it if he had a comfortable income. He’d welcome the time for other interests.”

“My uncle says Mr. Tyke is described as an apostolic man,” Dorothea said thoughtfully. She wished the zeal of early Christianity could be restored, yet at the same time she felt a powerful desire to rescue Mr. Farebrother from earning money by games of chance.

“I wouldn’t claim Farebrother is apostolic,” said Lydgate. “His situation is rather different from the Apostles’. He’s simply a parson among parishioners whose lives he must try to improve. In practice, what people now call apostolic seems to mean impatience with anything in which the parson isn’t the leading figure. I see something of that in Mr. Tyke at the Hospital. Much of his teaching amounts to pinching people hard to make them uncomfortably aware of his presence. Besides, an apostolic man at Lowick! He’d have to decide, like St. Francis, that the birds needed preaching to.”

“That’s true,” said Dorothea. “It’s difficult to imagine what ideas our farmers and laborers get from the teaching they hear. I’ve been looking through a volume of Mr. Tyke’s sermons. Sermons like those would be useless at Lowick—I mean the ones about imputed righteousness and the prophecies of the Apocalypse. I’ve always thought about the different ways Christianity is taught. Whenever I find a way that makes it a greater blessing than any other, I hold to that as the truest. I mean the teaching that embraces the most goodness of every kind, and allows the most people to share in it. Surely it’s better to forgive too much than condemn too much. But I’d like to meet Mr. Farebrother and hear him preach.”

“Please do,” said Lydgate. “I’m confident that will persuade you. He’s greatly loved, though he has enemies too. There are always people who can’t forgive a capable man for disagreeing with them. And winning money at cards really is a blemish. Of course, you don’t see many Middlemarch people, but Mr. Ladislaw, who sees Mr. Brooke constantly, is a close friend of Mr. Farebrother’s old ladies. He’d gladly sing the Vicar’s praises. One of them—his aunt, Miss Noble—is a wonderfully quaint picture of goodness that never thinks of itself. Ladislaw sometimes escorts her about. I met them in a back street one day. You know how Ladislaw looks—a sort of Daphnis in a coat and waistcoat. With that little old maid reaching up to his arm, they looked like a pair who’d stepped out of a romantic comedy. Still, the best evidence about Farebrother is to meet him and hear him.”

Fortunately this conversation took place in Dorothea’s private sitting room. Nobody else was there to make Lydgate’s innocent mention of Ladislaw painful to her. As usually happened with personal gossip, Lydgate had entirely forgotten Rosamond’s remark that she thought Will adored Mrs. Casaubon. Just then he cared only about recommending the Farebrother family. He had deliberately emphasized the worst things that could be said about the Vicar in order to anticipate objections. He had scarcely seen Ladislaw in the weeks since Mr. Casaubon’s death, and no rumor had warned him that mentioning Mr. Brooke’s confidential secretary to Mrs. Casaubon might be dangerous. After he left, his picture of Ladislaw lingered in Dorothea’s mind, competing with the question of the Lowick living. What was Will Ladislaw thinking of her? Would he hear the fact that made her cheeks burn as they never had before? How would he feel when he knew? Yet she could picture perfectly his smile as he looked down at the little old maid. An Italian with white mice! On the contrary, he was someone who could enter into anyone’s feelings, accepting the pressure of their thoughts instead of forcing his own upon them with iron resistance.

chapters.title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter LI
paragraphs: Ladislaw had still heard no gossip about Mr. Casaubon’s will. The dissolution of Parliament and the coming election filled the air, like the competing din of traveling shows at the old fairs and festivals; more private disturbances attracted little attention. The famous “dry election” was approaching, when the depth of public feeling could be measured by how low the tide of drink had fallen. Will Ladislaw was among the busiest people just then. Although Dorothea’s widowhood was constantly on his mind, he had no desire to discuss it. When Lydgate sought him out to report their conversation about the Lowick living, he answered rather sharply—

“Why bring me into it? I never see Mrs. Casaubon, and I’m unlikely to while she’s at Freshitt. I don’t go there. It’s Tory territory: the ‘Pioneer’ and I are about as welcome as a poacher with his gun.”

In fact, Will had become especially sensitive after noticing a change in Mr. Brooke. Previously Brooke had wanted him at the Grange more often than Will himself cared to go; now he seemed to arrange matters so that Will went there as little as possible. This was Mr. Brooke’s evasive concession to Sir James Chettam’s indignant protests. Will, alert to the faintest suggestion of this sort, concluded that he was being kept from the Grange because of Dorothea. So her friends were suspicious of him? Their fears were wholly unnecessary. If they imagined he would present himself as a penniless adventurer courting a wealthy woman’s favor, they were badly mistaken.

Will had never fully understood the gulf between himself and Dorothea until now, when he stood at its edge and saw her on the opposite side. With some inward fury he began considering leaving the neighborhood. He could show no further interest in her without exposing himself to unpleasant accusations—perhaps even in her own mind, which others might try to poison.

“We’re separated for ever,” Will told himself. “I might as well be in Rome; she couldn’t be any further away.” But what we call despair is often merely the painful impatience of hope denied its nourishment. There were plenty of reasons to stay—public reasons for remaining at his post in a crisis, instead of abandoning Mr. Brooke just when he needed coaching for the election and so much direct and indirect canvassing remained to be done. Will disliked deserting his own chessmen in the middle of a game. Any candidate on the right side might help secure a majority, even if his brains and backbone were as soft as a gentleman’s bearing would allow. Coaching Mr. Brooke was difficult: he had to be kept steadily committed to voting for the actual Reform Bill, instead of insisting on his independence and his ability to pull back in time. Mr. Farebrother’s prediction of a fourth candidate “in the bag” had not yet come true. Neither the Parliamentary Candidate Society nor any other body watching for ways to secure a reforming majority saw a difficulty worth intervening in while a second reform candidate, Mr. Brooke, might win a seat at his own expense. The contest remained entirely between Pinkerton, the old Tory member; Bagster, the new Whig member elected last time; and Mr. Brooke, the future independent member, who would bind himself to a party only on this occasion. Mr. Hawley and his allies would devote all their strength to electing Pinkerton. Brooke could succeed only through voters casting their sole vote for him and leaving Bagster behind, or through turning Tory votes into Reform votes. Naturally, the second method was preferable.

The hope of converting voters dangerously distracted Mr. Brooke. He believed wavering voters might be attracted by wavering statements; moreover, whenever opposing arguments resurfaced in his memory, his mind tended to catch on them again. Both habits caused Will Ladislaw considerable trouble.

“There are tactics in these matters, you know,” Mr. Brooke said. “Meeting people halfway—moderating your views—saying, ‘Well now, there’s something in that,’ and so forth. I agree this is a special occasion—the country expressing its own will—political unions—that sort of thing. But sometimes we use rather too sharp a knife, Ladislaw. Take these ten-pound householders: why ten? Draw a line somewhere, yes—but why exactly ten? Once you examine it, that’s a difficult question.”

“Of course it is,” Will said impatiently. “But if you’re going to wait for a logically perfect Bill, you’ll have to stand as a revolutionary, and I doubt Middlemarch would elect you then. This is no time to sit on the fence.”

Mr. Brooke always ended by agreeing with Ladislaw, whom he still regarded as a kind of Burke with a dash of Shelley. Before long, however, the wisdom of his own methods reasserted itself, and he returned to them full of hope. At this stage he was in excellent spirits, even when required to advance large sums of money. His powers of persuasion had not yet faced anything harder than a chairman’s speech introducing other speakers, or a conversation with a Middlemarch voter. He came away from these encounters feeling he was a born tactician, and regretting that he had not entered this field sooner. With Mr. Mawmsey, though, he felt some sense of defeat. Mr. Mawmsey was a leading Middlemarch representative of that great social force, the retail trader, and naturally one of the borough’s most uncertain voters. Personally he was happy to supply equally good tea and sugar to reformers and their opponents, and to agree impartially with both. Like the burgesses of earlier days, he felt that having to elect members of Parliament was a heavy burden on a town. Even if it were safe to encourage every party’s hopes beforehand, in the end he would have to disappoint respectable customers whose names appeared in his accounts. Mr. Brooke of Tipton regularly placed large orders with him. On the other hand, many members of Pinkerton’s committee had opinions backed by substantial grocery purchases. Judging that Mr. Brooke was not too “clever in his intellects,” Mr. Mawmsey thought him more likely to forgive a grocer pressured into voting against him. In his back parlor, he therefore spoke confidentially.

“Look at Reform from a family point of view, sir,” he said, pleasantly smiling and jingling the small silver coins in his pocket. “Will it support Mrs. Mawmsey and help her raise six children when I’m gone? I ask the question _fictiously_, knowing what the answer must be. Very well, sir. Tell me what a husband and father is to do when gentlemen come in and say, ‘Please yourself, Mawmsey, but if you vote against us, I’ll buy my groceries elsewhere. When I sweeten my drink, I like to know I’m serving my country by supporting tradesmen of the right political color.’ Those exact words have been spoken to me, sir, from the very chair you’re sitting in. Not by your honorable self, Mr. Brooke, of course.”

“No, no, no—that’s narrow-minded, you know. Until my butler complains about your goods, Mr. Mawmsey,” Mr. Brooke reassured him, “until I hear you’re sending bad sugar, spices—that sort of thing—I shall never tell him to shop elsewhere.”
“Sir, your humble servant, and much obliged,” said Mr. Mawmsey, feeling that politics had become a little clearer. “It would be a pleasure to vote for a gentleman who speaks so honorably.”

“Well, Mr. Mawmsey, you’d find it was the right thing to join our side. Reform will affect everyone eventually—a thoroughly popular measure. A sort of alphabet, you know, which must come first before you can move on. I quite agree that you must think of the family. But there’s public spirit to consider. We’re all one family, you know—we all share one cupboard. A vote, for instance: it might help men make their fortunes at the Cape. There’s no telling what a vote may achieve.” Mr. Brooke ended with a sense of drifting a little out to sea, though he still enjoyed the voyage. Mr. Mawmsey’s reply brought him sharply to a halt.

“Excuse me, sir, but I can’t afford that. When I vote, I must know what I’m doing. With respect, I must consider the effect on my till and my ledger. Prices, I’ll admit, are something nobody can fully account for. The sudden drops after you’ve bought a supply of currants—and currants won’t keep—I’ve never understood the rights and wrongs of that myself. A rebuke to human pride, it is. But as for one family, I hope we’ll still have debtors and creditors. They’re not going to reform that out of existence, or I’d vote to keep things as they are. Personally, few men have less cause to demand change than I do—for myself and my family, that is. I’m not a man with nothing to lose. I mean my standing in the parish and my private business, and nothing concerning your honorable self or your custom. You were kind enough to say you wouldn’t withdraw that, whichever way I voted, so long as the goods supplied were satisfactory.”
Afterwards Mr. Mawmsey went upstairs and boasted to his wife that he had rather outwitted Brooke of Tipton. Going to the poll no longer troubled him quite so much.

On this occasion Mr. Brooke did not boast of his tactics to Ladislaw. Will, for his part, was happy to believe he had no involvement in canvassing except through reasoned argument, and used no less honorable instrument than knowledge. Naturally, Mr. Brooke had agents who understood the Middlemarch voter and knew how to recruit his ignorance in favor of the Bill. Their methods were remarkably similar to those for recruiting it against the Bill. Will closed his ears. Sometimes Parliament could scarcely carry on if we imagined its processes too vividly; the same is true of the rest of our lives, even our food and clothes. There were enough dirty-handed men in the world to handle dirty business. Will assured himself that his own part in getting Mr. Brooke elected would be entirely innocent.

Still, he seriously doubted whether this way of helping secure a majority for the right side would succeed. He had written several speeches and sets of speaking notes. But he was beginning to see that if Mr. Brooke’s mind had to carry a train of thought, it would drop it, run off looking for it, and struggle to return. Collecting documents is one way of serving your country; remembering what they contain is another. No! The only way to force Mr. Brooke to think of the right arguments at the right moment was to feed him so many of them that nothing else would fit in his brain. Finding space was the difficulty: so much had already been stored there. Mr. Brooke himself remarked that his ideas tended to get in the way when he spoke.

Ladislaw’s coaching would shortly be tested. Before nomination day Mr. Brooke was to explain his position to Middlemarch’s worthy electors from the White Hart’s balcony. It occupied a useful angle of the marketplace, overlooking a broad space and two streets converging upon it. The May morning was fine, and the outlook promising. An agreement between Bagster’s committee and Brooke’s seemed possible. Mr. Bulstrode, Mr. Standish in his capacity as a Liberal lawyer, and manufacturers including Mr. Plymdale and Mr. Vincy gave Brooke’s committee a weight nearly equal to that of Mr. Hawley and his associates, who met for Pinkerton at the Green Dragon. Mr. Brooke knew that six months of improving his conduct as a landlord had blunted the “Trumpet’s” attacks. Hearing a few cheers as he drove into town, he felt fairly light-hearted beneath his buff waistcoat. Yet at critical occasions, every moment often seems comfortably far away until the last one arrives.
“This looks promising, eh?” said Mr. Brooke as people gathered. “I’ll have a good audience, at least. I enjoy this—a crowd made up of one’s own neighbors, you know.”

Unlike Mr. Mawmsey, Middlemarch’s weavers and tanners had never considered Mr. Brooke a neighbor. They felt no more attachment to him than if he had arrived in a box from London. Nevertheless, they listened fairly quietly to the speakers introducing him. One, a political figure from Brassing who had come to explain Middlemarch’s duty, spoke at such length that it was alarming to wonder what he could leave the candidate to say. Meanwhile the crowd thickened. As the political personage approached his conclusion, Mr. Brooke experienced a remarkable change in his feelings. Outwardly he continued handling his eyeglass, fiddling with the papers before him and chatting to his committee, as though wholly indifferent to when he was called upon.

“I’ll have another sherry, Ladislaw,” he said casually to Will, standing close behind him. Will soon supplied the supposed restorative. It was a poor choice. Mr. Brooke drank little, and quickly taking a second glass so soon after the first startled his system, scattering his energies instead of concentrating them. Do feel sorry for him. So many English gentlemen make themselves miserable giving speeches for wholly private purposes! Mr. Brooke wished to serve his country by standing for Parliament—something that may also be done for private purposes, certainly, but once undertaken it absolutely requires speeches.

The opening did not worry him. He was certain of that; he would have it ready, neatly cut and finished as a few couplets from Pope. Getting aboard would be easy. The prospect of the open sea afterwards was frightening. “And questions,” suggested the demon beginning to stir in his stomach, “someone might ask questions about the schedules.—Ladislaw,” he went on aloud, “pass me the notes on the schedules, will you?”

When Mr. Brooke stepped onto the balcony, the cheers easily balanced the yells, groans, brays and other expressions of opposing views. Indeed, these were so restrained that Mr. Standish, an old campaigner, remarked into the nearest ear, “By God, this looks dangerous! Hawley’s planned something deeper than this.” Still, the cheering was encouraging. No candidate could have looked more amiable than Mr. Brooke, his notes in his breast pocket, his left hand resting on the railing and his right playing with his eyeglass. His most noticeable features were the buff waistcoat, closely clipped fair hair and uncommitted expression. He began confidently enough.
“Gentlemen—electors of Middlemarch!”
This was exactly the proper beginning, and a brief pause after it seemed quite natural.
“I’m extraordinarily pleased to be here. I’ve never felt so proud and happy in my life—never so happy, you know.”

That was a bold figure of speech, though not quite the right one. Unfortunately his polished opening had vanished. Even Pope’s couplets may become “fallings from us, vanishings” when fear grips us and a glass of sherry rushes like smoke through our thoughts. Standing at the window behind him, Ladislaw thought, “That’s finished it. Our only hope is that since the best thing doesn’t always work, floundering might work for once.” Mr. Brooke, deprived of other guides, fell back on himself and his qualifications—always a suitable, graceful subject for a candidate.

“My good friends, I’m your near neighbor. You’ve known me as a magistrate for years. I’ve always examined public questions closely—machinery, for example, and machine-breaking. Many of you work with machinery, and I’ve been studying that lately. Breaking machines won’t do, you know. Everything must continue—trade, manufacturing, commerce, exchanging staple goods—all that. Since Adam Smith, it has to continue. We must survey the whole globe: ‘Observation with extensive view’ must look everywhere, ‘from China to Peru,’ as someone says. Johnson, I think—‘The Rambler,’ you know. I’ve done that myself, to a point—not as far as Peru. But I haven’t always stayed at home; I saw that wouldn’t do. I’ve visited the Levant, where some of your Middlemarch goods are sold—and the Baltic too. Now, the Baltic.”

Sailing among his memories like this, Mr. Brooke might have proceeded comfortably enough and returned from the furthest seas without difficulty. But the enemy had arranged a devilish intervention. At the very same moment, almost directly opposite him and less than ten yards away, an effigy of himself rose above the crowd’s shoulders. Buff waistcoat, eyeglass and neutral face were painted on cloth. With it came an echo of his words, parrot-like and shrill as Punch, apparently floating in the air like a cuckoo’s call. Everyone looked up at the open windows where the two streets met, but they were either empty or occupied by laughing spectators. Even the most innocent echo sounds impishly mocking when it follows a solemn, persistent speaker. This echo was far from innocent. It lacked a natural echo’s precision, but maliciously selected the words it caught. By the time it repeated “Now, the Baltic,” the laughter rippling through the crowd became a general roar. Only party loyalties and the great public cause which tangled circumstances had attached to “Mr. Brooke of Tipton” kept his own committee from joining in. Mr. Bulstrode sternly demanded to know what the new police were doing. But one could hardly arrest a voice, and attacking the effigy would send an ambiguous message, since Hawley probably intended it to be pelted.

Mr. Brooke himself was scarcely capable of noticing anything except the general flight of ideas from his own mind. His ears even rang a little. He alone had not yet properly registered either the echo or his own image. Few things imprison our perceptions more completely than anxiety over what to say next. He heard the laughter, but had expected Tory attempts at disruption. Besides, he was now excited by the tingling sense that his lost introduction was returning to bring him home from the Baltic.

“That reminds me,” he continued, slipping one hand casually into a side pocket, “if I needed a precedent, you know—though we never need a precedent for doing right—there’s Chatham, for instance. I can’t say I would have supported Chatham, or Pitt—the younger Pitt. He wasn’t a man of ideas, and ideas are what we need, you know.”
“Damn your ideas! We want the Bill!” shouted a rough voice from below.

The unseen Punch, which until then had followed Mr. Brooke, instantly repeated, “Damn your ideas! We want the Bill!” Laughter burst out louder than ever. For the first time, being silent himself, Mr. Brooke distinctly heard the mocking echo. But it seemed to be mocking the man who had interrupted him, which was encouraging. He therefore replied pleasantly—

“There’s something in what you say, my good friend. Why else do we gather, except to speak our minds—freedom of opinion, freedom of the press, liberty—all that? Now, the Bill—you shall have the Bill.” He paused to fit his eyeglass and draw the paper from his breast pocket, feeling that he was becoming practical and specific. The invisible Punch took up the words—
“You shall have the bill, Mr. Brooke: for one election contest, with a seat outside Parliament, as delivered—five thousand pounds, seven shillings and fourpence.”

Amid the roaring laughter, Mr. Brooke flushed and dropped his eyeglass. Looking round in confusion, he caught sight of his effigy, now closer than before. A moment later he saw it woefully splattered with eggs. His courage rose a little, and so did his voice.

“Clowning, tricks, ridicule as the test of truth—all very well—” At this point a disagreeable egg broke on Mr. Brooke’s shoulder, while the echo repeated, “All very well.” A shower of eggs followed, mostly aimed at the effigy, but occasionally striking the original as though by accident. Fresh men streamed into the crowd. Whistles, screams, bellows and fifes swelled the uproar, made louder still by the shouting and struggling of those trying to suppress it. No voice could have carried above such a din. Unpleasantly anointed, Mr. Brooke abandoned his position. The defeat would have been less maddening had it been less playful and schoolboyish. A serious assault, which a reporter “can aver that it endangered the learned gentleman’s ribs,” or respectfully describe as leaving “the soles of that gentleman’s boots having been visible above the railing,” might offer more consolation.

Mr. Brooke returned to the committee room, saying as lightly as he could, “That’s rather too bad, you know. I’d have won their attention eventually, but they gave me no time. I’d have explained the Bill in due course, you know,” he added with a glance at Ladislaw. “Still, it’ll all come right at the nomination.”
There was no unanimous confidence that it would. On the contrary, the committee looked grim, while the political visitor from Brassing wrote busily, apparently devising fresh plans.

“Bowyer was behind it,” Mr. Standish said evasively. “I’m as certain as if he’d advertised himself. He’s exceptionally good at ventriloquism, and by God, he did that exceptionally well! Hawley’s been inviting him to dinner lately. Bowyer has a fund of talent.”
“Well, Standish, you never mentioned him. Otherwise I’d have invited him myself,” said poor Mr. Brooke, who had done a great deal of inviting for his country’s sake.
“There’s no more contemptible fellow in Middlemarch than Bowyer,” Ladislaw said angrily. “Yet it always seems to be the contemptible fellows who tip the balance.”

Will was thoroughly angry with himself as well as with his employer. He shut himself in his rooms, half resolved to abandon both Mr. Brooke and the “Pioneer.” Why stay? If the impassable gulf between himself and Dorothea could ever be bridged, it would be by leaving and winning a completely different position, not by remaining here and sinking into deserved contempt as Brooke’s subordinate. Then came the youthful dream of the wonders he might achieve—in five years, say. Political writing and speaking would count for more now that public life was becoming broader and more national. They might win him enough distinction that he would no longer seem to be asking Dorothea to step down to his level. Five years—if only he knew she cared for him more than for other men; if only he could make her understand that he kept his distance until he could declare his love without degrading himself. Then he could leave readily and embark on a career that seemed perfectly plausible at twenty-five, according to the mind’s inward arrangement of things, where talent brings fame and fame brings every other delight. He could speak and write; he could master any subject he chose. He always intended to stand for reason and justice, bringing all his passion to their side. Why should he not one day rise above the crowd and feel he had earned his eminence? Certainly he would leave Middlemarch, go to London and prepare himself for distinction by “eating his dinners” as a student of law.

But not immediately—not until he and Dorothea had exchanged some kind of sign. He would not be satisfied until she understood why, even if he were the man she chose, he would refuse to marry her. So he must remain at his post and tolerate Mr. Brooke a little longer.

Before long, however, he had reason to suspect that Mr. Brooke had anticipated his wish to end their association. Outside delegations and voices closer to home had together persuaded that philanthropist to take an unusually decisive step for humanity’s benefit: he would withdraw in favor of another candidate, leaving that man the advantages of his canvassing organization. Mr. Brooke called this a strong measure, but remarked that his health could bear less excitement than he had supposed.

“I’ve had some discomfort in my chest. One mustn’t push that too far,” he explained to Ladislaw. “I must pull back. Poor Casaubon was a warning, you know. I’ve advanced some substantial sums, but I’ve dug a channel. It’s rather rough work, this electioneering, eh, Ladislaw? I dare say you’re tired of it. Still, we’ve dug a channel with the ‘Pioneer’—set things going, and so forth. A more ordinary man than you could keep it going now—someone more ordinary, you know.”
“Do you want me to give it up?” Will asked, color rushing into his face. He rose from the writing table and paced three steps with his hands in his pockets. “I’m ready to do so whenever you wish.”

“As for wishing, my dear Ladislaw, you know how highly I rate your abilities. But I’ve been discussing the ‘Pioneer’ with some men on our side. They’re inclined to take it over—reimburse me to some extent—and run it themselves. Under the circumstances, you might prefer to leave—find a better field for your talents. These people might not appreciate you as I always have, as an alter ego, a right hand. Though I’ve always expected you to go on to something else. I’m thinking of a little trip to France. But I’ll write whatever introductions you need, you know—to Althorpe and people like that. I’ve met Althorpe.”
“I’m extremely obliged to you,” Ladislaw replied proudly. “Since you’re parting with the ‘Pioneer,’ I needn’t trouble you with my own plans. I may decide to stay here for the present.”

Once Mr. Brooke had gone, Will told himself, “The rest of the family have been pressing him to get rid of me, and now he doesn’t mind if I leave. I’ll stay as long as I please. I’ll go when I choose, not because they’re afraid of me.”

chapters.title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter LII
paragraphs:
“His heart
The lowliest duties on itself did lay.”
—WORDSWORTH.

On the June evening when Mr. Farebrother learned that the Lowick living was his, joy filled the old-fashioned parlor. Even the portraits of the great lawyers seemed to look on approvingly. His mother left her tea and toast untouched. She sat with her customary pretty primness, revealing her feelings only through flushed cheeks and shining eyes—that touching, fleeting resemblance an old woman can suddenly bear to her distant younger self. She said firmly—
“The greatest comfort, Camden, is knowing you’ve earned it.”

“When a man gets a good position, mother, he has to earn half of it afterwards,” her son replied, overflowing with pleasure and making no attempt to hide it. His happiness had an active quality. It seemed energetic enough not merely to shine from his face, but to illuminate busy visions within. His glances appeared full of thoughts as well as delight.

“Now, aunt,” he continued, rubbing his hands and turning to Miss Noble, who was making soft little noises like a beaver, “there’ll always be sugar-candy on the table for you to steal for the children. And you’ll have any number of new stockings to give away, while you darn your own more than ever!”
Miss Noble nodded at her nephew with a quiet, slightly frightened laugh. On the strength of his advancement, she had already slipped another lump of sugar into her basket.
“As for you, Winny,” the Vicar continued, “I shan’t object to your marrying any bachelor in Lowick—Mr. Solomon Featherstone, for instance—as soon as I discover you’re in love with him.”

Miss Winifred had been gazing at her brother and weeping freely all this time; that was how she expressed joy. Smiling through her tears, she said, “You must show me how, Cam. _You_ must get married now.”
“Gladly! But who’s in love with me? I’m a shabby old fellow,” said the Vicar. He stood, pushed back his chair and looked himself over. “What do you think, mother?”
“You’re a handsome man, Camden, though your father cut a finer figure,” the old lady answered.
“I wish you’d marry Miss Garth, brother,” said Miss Winifred. “She’d make life at Lowick so cheerful.”

“Very fine! You speak as though young women were tied up for us to choose from, like poultry at a market—as though I had only to ask and anyone would accept me,” said the Vicar, choosing to name no particular woman.
“We don’t want just anyone,” Miss Winifred replied. “But _you’d_ like Miss Garth, wouldn’t you, mother?”

“Whoever my son chooses will be my choice,” said Mrs. Farebrother with stately discretion. “A wife would be very welcome, Camden. You’ll want to play whist at home when we move to Lowick, and Henrietta Noble has never been a whist player.” Mrs. Farebrother invariably bestowed that magnificent name on her tiny old sister.
“I won’t need whist any longer, mother.”

“Why ever not, Camden? In my day, whist was considered a perfectly proper amusement for a good churchman,” said Mrs. Farebrother. She knew nothing of what whist meant to her son, and spoke rather sharply, as though he were dangerously encouraging some new doctrine.
“I’ll be too busy for it. I’ll have two parishes,” the Vicar replied, preferring not to debate the game’s virtues.

He had already told Dorothea, “I don’t consider myself obliged to give up St. Botolph’s. If I give someone else most of its income, that’s enough of a protest against the practice of holding several livings, which they’re trying to reform. Using power well takes more strength than surrendering it.”

“I’ve thought about that,” Dorothea said. “For one’s own sake, I think giving up power and money would be easier than keeping them. It seems quite inappropriate that I should control this appointment, yet I felt I ought not to let someone else exercise the right for me.”
“Then it’s my responsibility to act in a way that won’t make you regret having that power,” said Mr. Farebrother.

His was a nature whose conscience became more active when life’s burdens stopped chafing. He made no show of humility about it, but privately felt rather ashamed. His conduct had included lapses which others, who received no comfortable livings, had avoided.

“I often used to wish I’d chosen something other than the Church,” he told Lydgate. “But perhaps I’d do better to make myself as good a clergyman as I can. That’s the comfortably provided clergyman’s view, you see,” he finished with a smile. “It makes difficulties much simpler.”

At that moment the Vicar really did feel his duties would be easy. But Duty has a habit of behaving unexpectedly—rather like a heavy friend we have cordially invited to stay, who then breaks his leg inside our gates.
Scarcely a week later, Duty appeared in his study disguised as Fred Vincy, home from Omnibus College with his bachelor’s degree.

“I’m ashamed to trouble you, Mr. Farebrother,” Fred said, his fair, open face asking indulgence. “But you’re the only friend I can turn to for advice. I told you everything before, and you were so kind that I can’t help coming back.”
“Sit down, Fred. I’ll listen, and help in any way I can,” said the Vicar. He continued packing the small objects he was preparing for the move.

“I wanted to tell you—” Fred hesitated, then plunged ahead. “I could enter the Church now. Honestly, wherever I look, I can’t see anything else I could do. I don’t like the idea, but I know it’s terribly hard on my father to say that after he’s spent so much on educating me for it.” He paused again, then repeated, “And I can’t see anything else I could do.”
“I did speak to your father about it, Fred, but I got nowhere. He said it was too late. Still, you’ve crossed one bridge now. What other difficulties stand in your way?”

“Only that I don’t like it. I don’t like theology, or preaching, or having to look solemn. I enjoy riding across country and doing what other men do. I don’t mean I want to behave badly in any way. I simply have no taste for the things people expect from a clergyman. But what else is there? My father can’t give me any capital, or I could take up farming. There’s no place for me in his business. And obviously I can’t begin studying law or medicine now, when he needs me to earn something. People say I ought not to enter the Church, but they might as well tell me to head off into the wilderness.”
Fred’s voice had become a complaining protest. Mr. Farebrother might have smiled if he had not been so occupied with imagining what Fred had left unsaid.
“Do you have any doubts about doctrine—about the Articles?” he asked, making a determined effort to consider the question solely in Fred’s interests.

“No. I suppose the Articles are right. I haven’t any arguments against them, and much better, cleverer men than me accept them completely. I’d feel rather ridiculous claiming scruples of that kind, as though I were qualified to judge,” Fred said simply.
“Then I imagine you’ve considered that you might make a decent parish priest without being much of a theologian?”
“Of course, if I have to be a clergyman, I’ll try to do my duty, even if I don’t enjoy it. Do you think anyone ought to blame me?”

“For entering the Church in these circumstances? That depends on your conscience, Fred—on how thoroughly you’ve weighed the cost and understood what the position will demand. All I can say about myself is that I’ve always been too lax, and it has troubled me.”

“There’s another difficulty,” Fred said, flushing. “I didn’t tell you before, although perhaps some things I said made you guess. There’s someone I’m very fond of. I’ve loved her since we were children.”
“Miss Garth, I assume?” said the Vicar, studying some labels intently.
“Yes. If she’d have me, I wouldn’t mind anything. I know I could be a good fellow then.”
“And you believe she feels the same?”

“She won’t ever say so. Some time ago she made me promise not to bring it up again. And she’s particularly opposed to my becoming a clergyman—I know that much. But I can’t give her up. I really do think she cares for me. I saw Mrs. Garth last night. She said Mary was staying with Miss Farebrother at Lowick Rectory.”
“Yes, she’s kindly helping my sister. Would you like to go there?”
“No. I want to ask you an enormous favor. I’m ashamed to bother you like this, but Mary might listen if you spoke to her about it—about my entering the Church, I mean.”
“That’s a delicate undertaking, my dear Fred. I would have to assume your attachment to her, and approaching the matter as you wish would amount to asking whether she returns your feelings.”
“That’s exactly what I want her to tell you,” Fred said bluntly. “Until I know how she feels, I don’t know what to do.”
“You mean her answer would guide your decision about entering the Church?”
“If Mary said she’d never have me, I might as well go wrong one way as another.”
“That’s nonsense, Fred. Men survive their love, but they don’t outlive the consequences of reckless behavior.”
“Not love like mine. I can’t remember a time when I didn’t love Mary. Giving her up would be like learning to live on wooden legs.”
“Might she resent my interference?”

“No, I’m certain she wouldn’t. She respects you more than anyone. She wouldn’t put you off with jokes, the way she does me. I couldn’t have told anyone else, of course, or asked anyone but you to speak to her. Nobody else could be such a friend to us both.” Fred paused, then added rather plaintively, “And she ought to recognize that I worked to pass my degree. She ought to believe I’d make an effort for her.”
There was a brief silence. Then Mr. Farebrother set down his work and held out his hand to Fred.
“All right, my boy. I’ll do as you ask.”
That same day Mr. Farebrother rode to Lowick parsonage on the horse he had recently acquired. “Clearly I’m an old stem,” he thought. “The young shoots are pushing me aside.”

He found Mary in the garden, collecting roses and scattering their petals over a sheet. The sun was sinking, and tall trees cast shadows across the grassy paths where she walked without a bonnet or parasol. She did not notice the Vicar approaching over the grass. She had just bent to scold a small black-and-tan terrier which insisted on walking over the sheet and sniffing the petals as she dropped them. Holding his front paws in one hand, she raised a finger of the other. The dog wrinkled his forehead and looked embarrassed. “Fly, Fly, I’m ashamed of you,” Mary was saying in her deep, serious voice. “This isn’t how a sensible dog behaves. Anyone would think you were a foolish young gentleman.”
“You show young gentlemen no mercy, Miss Garth,” said the Vicar, now only two yards away.
Mary straightened abruptly and blushed. “Reasoning with Fly always works,” she said with a laugh.
“But reasoning with young gentlemen doesn’t?”
“With some, I suppose. After all, some grow into excellent men.”
“I’m pleased you’ll admit that, because I’ve come to interest you in a young gentleman myself.”
“Not a foolish one, I hope,” said Mary, returning to her roses. Her heart had begun beating uncomfortably.

“No. Though perhaps wisdom isn’t his greatest strength—affection and sincerity are. Still, those two qualities contain more wisdom than people generally suppose. I hope that description tells you who I mean.”
“Yes, I think so,” Mary answered bravely. Her expression grew more serious and her hands turned cold. “You must mean Fred Vincy.”
“He’s asked me to consult you about entering the Church. I hope you won’t think I presumed too much by agreeing.”
“Quite the opposite, Mr. Farebrother,” said Mary. She stopped picking roses and folded her arms, but could not raise her eyes. “Whenever you have something to say to me, I feel honored.”

“Before we discuss that, though, let me mention something your father told me in confidence. It was, incidentally, the very evening I last carried a message from Fred, just after he’d gone back to college. Mr. Garth told me what happened on the night Featherstone died—your refusal to burn the will. He said your conscience troubled you because you had innocently prevented Fred from receiving his ten thousand pounds. I’ve remembered that. And I’ve learned something that may ease your mind—that may show you there’s no need for a sin-offering on that account.”

Mr. Farebrother paused and looked at her. He meant to give Fred every advantage. But he thought it best to clear her mind of the superstitious feelings that sometimes lead women to wrong a man by marrying him as an act of atonement. Mary’s cheeks had begun to burn, and she said nothing.

“What I mean is that your action made no actual difference to Fred’s prospects. I’ve learned that burning the later will wouldn’t have made the earlier one legally valid. If challenged, it wouldn’t have stood—and you can be certain it would have been challenged. On that point, then, you can set your mind at rest.”
“Thank you, Mr. Farebrother,” Mary said earnestly. “I’m very grateful that you remembered how I felt.”

“Now I can go on. As you know, Fred has his degree. He’s worked his way that far, and must now decide what to do. The question is so difficult that he’s inclined to follow his father’s wishes and enter the Church, although you know better than I how strongly he used to oppose it. I’ve questioned him, and I admit that, as things stand, I see no insurmountable objection to his becoming a clergyman. He says he could set himself to doing his best in that calling, on one condition. If that condition were met, I’d do everything I could to help him advance. In time—not immediately, of course—he could become my curate. There would be enough work for him that his salary would almost equal what I used to receive as Vicar. But, as I say, all this depends on one condition. He has confided in me, Miss Garth, and asked me to speak for him. That condition rests entirely on your feelings.”

Mary seemed so deeply affected that he paused, then said, “Shall we walk a little?” As they walked he added, “To put it plainly, Fred won’t do anything that might reduce his chance of your agreeing to marry him. But with that hope, he’ll do his best at any work you approve of.”

“I couldn’t possibly promise ever to marry him, Mr. Farebrother. But I certainly never will if he becomes a clergyman. Your proposal is immensely kind and generous. I wouldn’t dream of questioning your judgment. It’s only my girlish habit of seeing things in a mocking light,” Mary said. A playful sparkle returned to her answer, making its modesty still more charming.
“He wants me to tell him exactly what you think,” Mr. Farebrother replied.

“I couldn’t love a ridiculous man,” said Mary, choosing not to go deeper. “Fred has enough knowledge and common sense to earn respect in some useful worldly occupation, if he chooses. But I can’t picture him preaching, exhorting, pronouncing blessings or praying beside the sick without feeling I’m looking at a caricature. He’d enter the Church only for social standing, and nothing seems more contemptible to me than that sort of feeble-minded gentility. I used to feel the same about Mr. Crowse, with his vacant face, tidy umbrella and fussy little speeches. What right have men like that to represent Christianity—as though it were an institution for dressing idiots respectably—as though—” Mary stopped herself. She had been carried away as if speaking to Fred rather than Mr. Farebrother.
“Young women judge harshly. They don’t experience the pressure of action as men do—though perhaps I ought to except you. But surely you don’t place Fred Vincy as low as that?”
“Certainly not. He has plenty of sense. But I don’t think it would show if he became a clergyman. He’d be playing at a profession.”
“So your answer is definite? As a clergyman, he’d have no hope?”
Mary answered with a shake of her head.
“But suppose he faced all the difficulties of earning his living in another way. Would you give him hope to sustain him? Could he count on winning you?”

“I don’t think Fred needs to be told again what I’ve already said,” Mary replied with a trace of resentment. “I mean he shouldn’t ask these questions until he’s actually done something worthwhile, instead of saying he could.”

Mr. Farebrother remained silent for a minute or more. Then they turned and stopped beneath a maple’s shade at the end of a grassy path, and he said, “I understand that you resist any attempt to bind you. But either your feeling for Fred Vincy prevents you from becoming attached to someone else, or it doesn’t. Either he can rely on your remaining unmarried until he’s earned your hand, or he may be disappointed whatever he does. Forgive me, Mary—you know I used to question you on your catechism by that name. But when a woman’s affections affect the happiness of another life—of more than one life—I think the nobler course is complete openness and honesty.”

Now Mary was silent. It was not Mr. Farebrother’s manner that puzzled her, but his tone, with its grave, restrained emotion. The strange possibility flashed through her mind that he was referring to himself. She could not believe it, and felt ashamed even to imagine it. She had never supposed any man could love her except Fred, who had married her with a ring from an umbrella when she still wore little socks and strapped shoes. Still less had she imagined that she might matter to Mr. Farebrother, the cleverest man in her small circle. She had only time to sense how uncertain and perhaps illusory all this was. One thing, however, was clear and settled: her answer.

“Since you think it’s my duty, Mr. Farebrother, I’ll tell you: my feelings for Fred are too strong for me to give him up for anyone else. I could never be entirely happy knowing he was unhappy because he’d lost me. My gratitude to him is rooted so deeply—for always loving me best, and caring so much whenever I hurt myself, ever since we were tiny. I can’t imagine any new feeling weakening that. More than anything, I’d like to see him deserve everyone’s respect. But please tell him I won’t promise to marry him before then. It would shame and grieve my father and mother. He’s free to choose someone else.”

“Then I’ve fully carried out my commission,” said Mr. Farebrother, offering Mary his hand. “I’ll ride straight back to Middlemarch. With that hope before him, we’ll find Fred his proper place somehow. And I hope I’ll live to join your hands. God bless you!”

“Oh, do stay and let me give you some tea,” Mary pleaded. Tears filled her eyes. Something she could not name in his manner—something like a resolute effort to suppress pain—made her suddenly miserable, as she had once been on seeing her father’s hands tremble in distress.
“No, my dear, no. I must go back.”
Three minutes later the Vicar was on his horse again. He had generously fulfilled a duty far harder than giving up whist, or even writing penitential meditations.

chapters.title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter LIII
paragraphs:
It is but a shallow haste which concludeth insincerity from what
outsiders call inconsistency—putting a dead mechanism of “ifs” and
“therefores” for the living myriad of hidden suckers whereby the belief
and the conduct are wrought into mutual sustainment.

As Mr. Bulstrode hoped to acquire property in Lowick, he naturally had a particular wish that its new clergyman should be someone he fully approved of. Instead, just as he received the deeds making him owner of Stone Court, Mr. Farebrother formally assumed his duties in the quaint little church and preached his first sermon to the farmers, laborers and village craftsmen. Mr. Bulstrode understood this as punishment and warning for his own failings and those of the nation. He had no immediate intention of attending Lowick Church or living at Stone Court. He had bought the excellent farm and fine house simply as a retreat. Gradually he could add land and improve the dwelling, until taking up residence there would serve God’s glory. He could then withdraw partly from his business activities and place the influence of a local landowner more conspicuously behind Gospel truth. Providence might increase that influence through unexpected opportunities to purchase more land. The surprising ease with which he had obtained Stone Court seemed a strong divine guidance in this direction. Everyone had expected Mr. Rigg Featherstone to hold on to it as though it were Eden. Poor old Peter had expected as much himself. In imagination he had often gazed up through the turf above his grave and, unhindered by perspective, watched his frog-faced heir enjoying the fine old estate, to the perpetual astonishment and disappointment of the other survivors.

Yet how little we know what paradise would mean to our neighbors! We judge by our own wishes, and our neighbors do not always reveal even a hint of theirs. Cool, calculating Joshua Rigg had never allowed his father to suspect that Stone Court was anything less than his highest ambition; and he certainly had wanted to own it. But just as Warren Hastings looked at gold and thought of buying Daylesford, Joshua Rigg looked at Stone Court and thought of buying gold. His vision of supreme happiness was both precise and intense. Circumstances had given the vigorous greed he inherited a particular shape: he longed to be a moneychanger. Ever since his first employment as an errand boy in a seaport, he had gazed through moneychangers’ windows as other boys gazed into pastry shops. The fascination had gradually become a deep, exclusive passion. Once wealthy, he intended to do many things, including marry a genteel young woman; but these were incidental pleasures, dispensable to his imagination. The one delight his soul thirsted for was a moneychanger’s shop on a busy quay. He would sit surrounded by locks to which he alone held the keys, looking supremely cool as he handled the multiplying coins of every nation, while helpless Greed stared enviously through an iron grille. That passion had given him the strength to master all the knowledge needed to satisfy it. While others imagined he had settled at Stone Court for life, Joshua was thinking how soon he might settle on the North Quay, equipped with the finest safes and locks.

Enough of that. Our concern is Joshua Rigg’s sale as Mr. Bulstrode saw it. He interpreted it as an encouraging act of Providence, perhaps endorsing a purpose he had long entertained without outward encouragement. He did so cautiously, however, framing his thanksgiving in guarded terms. His doubts had nothing to do with what the event might mean for Joshua Rigg’s destiny. That belonged to unmapped territory outside Providence’s government, except perhaps under some imperfect colonial administration. Rather, Bulstrode reflected that this event too might be meant to chastise him, just as Mr. Farebrother’s appointment plainly was.

This was not something Mr. Bulstrode told other people to deceive them. It was what he told himself. It was as sincerely his explanation of events as any theory of yours, if you disagree with him, may be yours. The self-interest mixed into our theories does not make them insincere. Indeed, the more they satisfy our self-interest, the firmer our belief becomes.

Whether as approval or punishment, then, Mr. Bulstrode became owner of Stone Court barely fifteen months after Peter Featherstone’s death. What Peter would say “if he were worthy to know” became an endless, comforting topic among his disappointed relatives. The tables had turned on their dear departed brother. Solomon never tired of savoring how the cunning of circumstances had defeated Peter’s own cunning. Mrs. Waule enjoyed a melancholy triumph in this proof that inventing false Featherstones and disinheriting the true ones did not pay. When Sister Martha heard the news in the Chalky Flats, she said, “Dear, dear! Then the Almighty can’t have been so pleased with those almshouses after all.”

Affectionate Mrs. Bulstrode was especially pleased by the benefit Stone Court might bring her husband’s health. Hardly a day passed without his riding over to inspect some part of the farm with the bailiff. Evenings in that quiet place were delightful. Newly built hayricks scented the air, mingling with the fragrance of the luxuriant old garden. One evening, while the sun still stood above the horizon, burning like golden lamps among the great walnut branches, Mr. Bulstrode waited on horseback outside the front gate for Caleb Garth. They had arranged to meet so Caleb could advise about drainage in the stables; he was now in the rickyard consulting with the bailiff.

Mr. Bulstrode felt spiritually well disposed and unusually peaceful, thanks to his innocent recreation. His religious doctrine assured him he possessed no merit whatever. Yet that conviction can be held painlessly when one’s unworthiness takes no definite shape in memory, reviving the sting of shame or the ache of remorse. It can even bring intense satisfaction when the depth of our sins merely measures the depth of forgiveness and supplies conclusive proof that we are specially chosen instruments of God’s purpose. Memory has as many moods as temperament, changing its scenery like a diorama. At this moment the sunlight seemed to Mr. Bulstrode continuous with that of distant evenings when, as a very young man, he used to go preaching beyond Highbury. He would gladly have looked forward to such a service of exhortation now. The texts still existed, and so did his skill at explaining them. Caleb Garth’s return interrupted this brief reverie. Caleb too was mounted and had just shaken his bridle to set off when he exclaimed—
“Bless me! Who’s this fellow in black coming down the lane? He looks like one of those men you see hanging about after the races.”

Mr. Bulstrode turned his horse to look down the lane but said nothing. The approaching figure was our slight acquaintance Mr. Raffles. Nothing about him had changed except his black suit and crape hatband. He came within three yards of the riders. They saw recognition flash across his face as he swung his stick up, keeping his eyes on Mr. Bulstrode, and finally cried—

“By Jove, Nick, it is you! No mistaking you, though twenty-five years have played the devil with us both! How are you, eh? You didn’t expect to find _me_ here. Come on, shake hands.” Saying that Mr. Raffles was rather excited would merely have been another way of saying it was evening. Caleb Garth noticed a moment’s struggle and hesitation in Mr. Bulstrode. Then the banker coldly held out his hand and said—
“I certainly did not expect to encounter you in this isolated country spot.”

“It belongs to my stepson,” said Raffles, adopting a swaggering stance. “I’ve visited him here before. I’m not so surprised to see you, old fellow, because I picked up a letter—what you might call an act of Providence. Still, it’s remarkably lucky I’ve met you. I don’t particularly want to see my stepson. He’s not affectionate, and his poor mother’s dead now. To tell the truth, Nick, it was love for you that brought me. I came for your address, because—look!” He pulled a crumpled paper from his pocket.

Almost anyone except Caleb Garth might have lingered to hear more. This man’s acquaintance with Bulstrode suggested episodes in the banker’s life so unlike anything Middlemarch knew of him that they promised the fascination of a secret. Caleb, however, was unusual. Some tendencies generally strong in human beings scarcely existed in him, including curiosity about other people’s private affairs. If something discreditable might be discovered about a man, Caleb especially preferred not to know it. When he had to tell a subordinate that his misconduct had been found out, Caleb was more embarrassed than the offender. He now spurred his horse. “Good evening, Mr. Bulstrode. I must get home,” he said, and trotted off.

“You didn’t give your full address on this letter,” Raffles continued. “Not like the first-rate businessman you used to be. ‘The Shrubs’—that could be anywhere. You live nearby, eh? Given up the London concern altogether? Turned country squire, perhaps, with a rural mansion to invite me to? Lord, what a lot of years! The old lady must have been dead a good while—gone to glory without the pain of learning how poor her daughter was, eh? But by Jove, Nick! You look pale and pasty. Come along, if you’re heading home, I’ll walk beside you.”

Mr. Bulstrode’s habitual pallor had indeed become almost deathly. Five minutes earlier, the whole expanse of his life lay bathed in evening sunshine reaching back to the morning of memory. Sin had seemed a matter of doctrine and inward repentance; humiliation, a private exercise; the meaning of his actions, a question of inward vision shaped solely by spiritual relationships and ideas of God’s purposes. Now, as if conjured by some hideous magic, this loud, red-faced figure stood solidly and uncontrollably before him—the past made flesh, in a form of punishment he had never imagined. But Mr. Bulstrode’s mind was working, and he was not a man to speak or act rashly.
“I was on my way home,” he said, “but I can postpone my ride. You may rest here, if you wish.”
“Thank you,” Raffles replied with a grimace. “I don’t care to see my stepson just now. I’d rather come home with you.”
“If you mean Mr. Rigg Featherstone, your stepson no longer lives here. This is now my property.”

Raffles widened his eyes and gave a long, surprised whistle. “Well then, no objection. I’ve walked quite far enough from the coach road. I’ve never been much of a walker—or a rider, for that matter. Give me a smart carriage and a spirited cob. I’ve always been a little heavy in the saddle. What a pleasant surprise seeing me must be, old fellow!” he went on as they turned towards the house. “You don’t say so, but you never greeted your good fortune heartily. You were always thinking of improving the occasion—and you certainly had a gift for improving your luck.”
Mr. Raffles thoroughly enjoyed his own wit. He swung his leg with a swagger that rather strained his companion’s carefully judged patience.

“If I remember correctly,” Mr. Bulstrode said with cold anger, “our acquaintance years ago was not as intimate as you now presume, Mr. Raffles. I shall be more willing to provide whatever assistance you seek if you avoid a familiarity that never characterized our former dealings, and which more than twenty years apart can hardly justify.”

“You don’t like being called Nick? Why, in my heart I always called you Nick. Lost to sight, to memory dear! By Jove, my feelings for you have matured like fine old cognac. I hope there’s some in the house. Josh filled my flask generously last time.”

Mr. Bulstrode had not yet fully grasped that Raffles’s appetite for torment equaled even his appetite for cognac. Any sign of irritation simply gave him a fresh opening. But further objections were plainly useless. When Mr. Bulstrode instructed the housekeeper to accommodate his guest, he maintained a determined calm.
He could at least take comfort in knowing that this housekeeper had served Rigg too. She might suppose he was entertaining Raffles only as a friend of her former employer.
Once food and drink stood before the visitor in the paneled parlor, and nobody else remained in the room, Mr. Bulstrode said—

“Our habits differ so greatly, Mr. Raffles, that neither of us is likely to enjoy the other’s company. The sensible course, therefore, is to part as soon as possible. Since you say you wanted to see me, I assume you had some business to discuss. In the circumstances, however, I invite you to stay here tonight. I shall ride over early tomorrow—before breakfast, in fact—and hear whatever you wish to communicate.”

“Gladly,” said Raffles. “It’s comfortable here—a bit dull for a long stay, but I can manage one night with this good liquor and the prospect of seeing you again in the morning. You’re a much better host than my stepson. Josh held a bit of a grudge because I married his mother. But there’s never been anything between you and me except kindness.”

Hoping that drink accounted for much of Raffles’s peculiar blend of jollity and sneering, Mr. Bulstrode decided to say no more until he was sober. Yet as he rode home he saw with terrible clarity how difficult it would be to reach any dependable, lasting arrangement with this man. Inevitably he wanted to be rid of John Raffles, though his return could not be considered outside God’s plan. The spirit of evil might have sent him to threaten Mr. Bulstrode’s usefulness as an instrument of good, but the threat must have been permitted. This was a new kind of chastisement. His anguish differed profoundly from those hours when his struggle had remained safely private, ending in the assurance that his hidden misdeeds were forgiven and his services accepted. Even when he committed those deeds, had they not been half sanctified by his single-minded wish to devote himself and all he possessed to advancing the divine design? Was he now, after all, to become merely a stumbling stone and rock of offense? Who would understand the work taking place within him? Given an excuse to disgrace him, who would not throw his whole life and the truths he upheld into one heap of condemnation?

In his most private reflections, lifelong habit dressed Mr. Bulstrode’s most selfish fears in religious language about purposes beyond humanity. Yet even as we discuss the earth’s orbit and the solar system, what we feel and guide our movements by is the solid ground and the changing daylight. Now, beneath the automatic procession of theoretical phrases, he anticipated disgrace before his neighbors and his own wife. That expectation was as inward and unmistakable as the shivering ache of an approaching fever while we discuss pain in the abstract. Both the suffering of disgrace and the public judgment of it depend on how much a man previously claimed to be. To men whose only aim is avoiding serious crime, nothing short of the prisoner’s dock means disgrace. Mr. Bulstrode, however, had aspired to be an outstanding Christian.

It was only half past seven the next morning when he reached Stone Court again. The fine old place had never looked more inviting as a home. Great white lilies were blooming, and nasturtiums, their pretty leaves silvered with dew, trailed over the low stone wall. Even the surrounding sounds seemed to contain a peaceful heart. But for the owner, everything was spoiled as he paced the gravel outside, waiting for Mr. Raffles to come downstairs. He was condemned to breakfast with him.

Soon they sat together in the paneled parlor over tea and toast, all Raffles cared for at that hour. His morning self differed less from his evening self than Bulstrode had hoped. If anything, slightly lower spirits sharpened his pleasure in tormenting. Certainly his manners appeared more unpleasant in daylight.

“I have little time to spare, Mr. Raffles,” said the banker. He could scarcely do more than sip his tea and break his toast without eating it. “I should be obliged if you would state immediately why you wanted to see me. I assume you have a home elsewhere and will be glad to return to it.”

“Why, doesn’t a man with any heart want to see an old friend, Nick? I must call you Nick. We always called you young Nick when we knew you meant to marry the old widow. Some said you bore a handsome family resemblance to Old Nick, but that was your mother’s fault for naming you Nicholas. Aren’t you pleased to see me? I’d expected an invitation to stay at some pretty place of yours. My own home’s broken up since my wife died. I’m not particularly attached to anywhere. I’d settle hereabouts as readily as anywhere else.”
“May I ask why you came back from America? When you expressed such a strong desire to go, and were given sufficient money, I understood that as effectively a promise to remain there for life.”
“I never knew wanting to go somewhere meant wanting to stay. Still, I stayed about ten years. Staying longer didn’t suit me. And I shan’t go back, Nick.” Mr. Raffles looked at him and slowly winked.
“Do you want help setting up in business? What occupation do you follow now?”

“Thank you, my occupation is enjoying myself as much as possible. I don’t care to work any more. If I did anything, it would be a little traveling in tobacco—or something similar that brings a man into pleasant company. But I’d need an independent income to fall back on. That’s what I want. I’m not as strong as I used to be, Nick, though I’ve more color than you. I want independence.”
“That could be provided, if you undertook to stay away,” Mr. Bulstrode said, perhaps with too much eagerness beneath his voice.

“That’ll have to depend on my convenience,” Mr. Raffles replied coolly. “Why shouldn’t I make a few acquaintances here? I’m not ashamed to keep company with anyone. I left my portmanteau at the turnpike when I got off the coach. A change of linen—genuine, on my honor—not just shirt fronts and cuffs. And in this mourning suit, trouser straps and all, I’d do you credit among the local gentry.” He pushed his chair back and examined himself, especially the straps. His main object was to annoy Bulstrode, but he genuinely believed his current appearance would impress. In his opinion he was handsome and witty, and his style of mourning suggested substantial family connections.
“If you mean to depend on me in any way, Mr. Raffles,” Bulstrode said after a pause, “you must expect to comply with my wishes.”

“Ah, naturally,” said Raffles with mocking warmth. “Didn’t I always? Lord, you profited handsomely through me, and I received very little. I’ve often thought since that I might have done better by telling the old woman I’d found her daughter and grandchild. It would have suited my feelings better. I’ve a soft spot in my heart. But you’ve buried the old lady by now, I suppose, so it’s all the same to her. And you’ve made your fortune from that profitable business that was so blessed. Now you’re a gentleman, buying land and playing the country pasha. Still a Dissenter, eh? Still godly? Or have you joined the Church because it’s more respectable?”

This time Mr. Raffles’s slow wink and slightly protruding tongue were worse than a nightmare, precisely because Mr. Bulstrode knew this was no dream but waking misery. He felt a shuddering nausea and remained silent, earnestly weighing whether to let Raffles do as he pleased and simply denounce him as a slanderer. The fellow would soon prove disreputable enough that nobody would believe him. “Not if he tells an ugly truth about _you_,” his clearer consciousness answered. Besides, although keeping Raffles away seemed no wrong, Mr. Bulstrode recoiled from directly lying to deny true statements. Looking back at forgiven sins—or explaining questionable compliance with lax practices—was one thing. Deliberately committing himself to necessary falsehood was another.
Since Bulstrode said nothing, Raffles continued, making the fullest use of his time.

“By Jove, I’ve not had your luck! New York treated me damned badly. Those Yankees are cool customers. A man with gentlemanly feelings hasn’t a chance against them. I married after I returned—a nice woman in the tobacco trade, very fond of me. But business was limited, as we say. A friend had set her up there years before. Unfortunately, there was one son too many. Josh and I never got along. Still, I made the best of things, and I’ve always had my drink in good company. I’ve kept everything above board. I’m open as daylight. You won’t hold it against me that I didn’t find you sooner. I have a complaint that makes me rather slow about things. I thought you were still trading and praying away in London, but I couldn’t find you there. You see, though, I was sent to you, Nick—perhaps as a blessing to us both.”

He ended with a comic nasal whine. Nobody felt more intellectually superior to religious cant than Mr. Raffles. And if cunning that calculates on people’s basest feelings counts as intellect, he possessed his share. Beneath the blustering, teasing tone of his talk, his statements were evidently selected like moves in a chess game. Meanwhile Bulstrode had chosen his own move. Gathering his resolution, he said—

“You would do well to remember, Mr. Raffles, that a man can overreach himself in trying to gain an unfair advantage. I am under no obligation to you. Nevertheless, I am willing to provide a regular annuity, paid quarterly, for as long as you keep a promise to stay away from this neighborhood. The choice is yours. If you insist on remaining here, even briefly, you will receive nothing from me. I shall refuse to acknowledge you.”
“Ha, ha!” Raffles burst out theatrically. “That reminds me of a comical thief who refused to acknowledge the constable.”
“Your insinuations have no bearing on me, sir,” Bulstrode said with white-hot anger. “Neither you nor anyone else can give the law a hold over me.”
“You can’t take a joke, my good fellow. I only meant that _I’d_ never refuse to acknowledge _you_. But seriously, quarterly payments don’t quite suit me. I like my freedom.”

Raffles stood and strode across the room once or twice, swinging his leg and adopting the air of a man reflecting with authority. At last he stopped before Bulstrode. “I’ll tell you what! Give me a couple of hundred—come, that’s modest—and I’ll leave. On my honor! I’ll collect my portmanteau and go. But I won’t surrender my liberty for a miserable annuity. I’ll come and go wherever I choose. Perhaps it’ll suit me to stay away and correspond with a friend; perhaps it won’t. Have you got the money on you?”
“No, only one hundred,” Bulstrode said. Immediate relief was too welcome to reject because the future remained uncertain. “Give me an address, and I’ll send the rest.”
“No, I’ll wait until you bring it,” said Raffles. “I’ll take a walk and get something to eat. You’ll be back by then.”

Mr. Bulstrode’s weak body, shaken by everything he had endured since the previous evening, left him feeling utterly at the mercy of this loud, invulnerable man. Just then he grasped at temporary relief on any terms. He was rising to obey when Raffles raised a finger as though something had suddenly occurred to him.

“I did look for Sarah again, though I never told you. My conscience bothered me about that pretty young woman. I didn’t find her, but I learned her husband’s name and wrote it down. Then, damn it, I lost my pocketbook. Still, I’d recognize it if I heard it. My faculties are as good as in my prime, but names wear out, by Jove! Sometimes I’m no better than a damned tax form before the names are filled in. Anyway, if I hear of her or her family, I’ll tell you, Nick. Now she’s your stepdaughter, you’d like to help her.”
“Certainly,” said Mr. Bulstrode, his light-gray eyes as steady as usual. “Though that might limit my ability to assist you.”

As Bulstrode left, Raffles winked slowly at his retreating back. Then he turned to the window to watch the banker ride away, practically at his command. His lips curled into a smile, followed by a brief triumphant laugh.

“But what the devil was the name?” he soon muttered, scratching his head and drawing horizontal wrinkles across his forehead. He had not really cared about, or even considered, this lapse of memory until it occurred to him while inventing ways to torment Bulstrode.

“It began with L. Almost all l’s, I fancy,” he continued, feeling the elusive name almost within reach. But his grasp was too slight, and he soon tired of the mental pursuit. Few men were less patient with solitary occupation, or more dependent on constantly making themselves heard, than Mr. Raffles. He preferred spending his time in pleasant conversation with the bailiff and housekeeper. From them he learned as much as he wanted about Mr. Bulstrode’s standing in Middlemarch.

Even so, a dull interval eventually arose which required the relief of bread, cheese and ale. Sitting alone with these resources in the paneled parlor, Raffles suddenly slapped his knee and exclaimed, “Ladislaw!” The work of memory he had tried to initiate, then abandoned in despair, had suddenly completed itself without conscious effort. It is a common experience, as satisfying as a completed sneeze, even when the recovered name is worthless. Raffles immediately took out his pocketbook and wrote it down. He did not expect to use it; he simply wished to have it available if he ever needed it. He would not tell Bulstrode. Telling offered no immediate advantage, whereas to a mind like Mr. Raffles’s a secret always held the prospect of one.

Satisfied with his success, by three that afternoon he had collected his portmanteau at the turnpike and boarded the coach. Mr. Bulstrode’s view of Stone Court was cleared of an ugly black blot. But he was not freed from the fear that the blot might return and become inseparable even from his vision of his own hearth.

chapters.title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LIV
paragraphs:
“Negli occhi porta la mia donna Amore;
Per che si fa gentil ciò ch’ella mira:
Ov’ella passa, ogni uom ver lei si gira,
E cui saluta fa tremar lo core.
Sicchè, bassando il viso, tutto smore, E d’ogni suo difetto allor sospira: Fuggon dinanzi a lei Superbia ed Ira: Aiutatemi, donne, a farle onore.
